rows.official_claim_short: 'non-cryptographic'; spec: 'not meant to avoid intentional collisions'; passes SMHasher; collisions 'in line with the birthday paradox'; a secret 'makes it more difficult for an external actor to prepare an intentional collision'; known seed-dependent multicollisions for 17-240 B.
rows.official_claim_quote: xxHash is primarily designed for speed. It is labeled non-cryptographic, and is not meant to avoid intentional collisions (same digest for 2 different messages), or to prevent producing a message with a predefined digest. | It's possible to provide any blob of bytes as a "secret" to generate the hash. This makes it more difficult for an external actor to prepare an intentional collision. | DISCLAIMER: There are known *seed-dependent* multicollisions here due to multiplication by zero, affecting hashes of lengths 17 to 240. However, they are very unlikely. Keep this in mind when using the unseeded XXH3_64bits() variant: As with all unseeded non-cryptographic hashes, it does not attempt to defend itself against specially crafted inputs, only random inputs. | Finally, xxHash provides its own [massive collision tester](https://github.com/Cyan4973/xxHash/tree/dev/tests/collisions), able to generate and compare billions of hashes to test the limits of 64-bit hash algorithms. rows.official_claim_quote:
* MUM hash passes **all** [SMHasher](https://github.com/aappleby/smhasher) tests
  * For comparison, only 4 out of 15 non-cryptographic hash functions
    in SMHasher passes the tests, e.g. well known FNV, Murmur2,
    Lookup, and Superfast hashes fail the tests |   * MUM and VMUM are also *resistant* to preimage attack (finding a
    key with a given hash) 
    * To make hard moving to previous state values we use mostly 1-to-1 one way
      function `lo(x*C) + hi(x*C)` where C is a constant.  Brute force
      solution of equation `f(x) = a` probably requires `2^63` tries.
      Another used function equation `x ^ y = a` has a `2^64`
      solutions.  It complicates finding the overal solution further |   It is easy to generate data which makes the 1st operand of `_vmum`
  to be zero.  In this case whatever the second operand is, the hash
  will be generated the same.  So an adversary can generate a lot of
  data with the same hash

rows.official_claim_quote: Note that `komihash` is not cryptographically secure. In open systems and internal server-side data structures, it should be used only with a secret seed to minimize the risk of collision attacks (hash flooding). However, using the default seed (0) reduces overhead by 1-2 cycles/hash (depending on the compiler). | The function passes all [SMHasher](https://github.com/rurban/smhasher) and [SMHasher3](https://gitlab.com/fwojcik/smhasher3/-/tree/main/results) tests. The function was also tested with the [xxHash collision tester](https://github.com/Cyan4973/xxHash/tree/dev/tests/collisions) under various settings, and the collision statistics met expectations. | Another reason is that for a non-cryptographic hash function, this step provides no additional security. While it may seem to protect against simple "state-XOR" collision attacks, in practice it offers no protection given the power of [SAT solvers](https://github.com/pysathq/pysat). In less than a second, a SAT solver can forge a preimage that produces the required hash value. It is also important to note that in fast hash functions such as `komihash`, the input message completely determines the state variables and the result.

rows.official_claim_quote:
Note that `a5hash` functions are not cryptographically secure. To minimize the risk of a successful collision attack (hash flooding) in open systems and in server-side internal structures, they should only be used with a secret seed, and their output should not be exposed. This is especially important if a malicious party is likely to try to influence the hash outputs. However, if "blinding multiplication" (BM, state cancellation) occurs at a random iteration, these functions immediately recover from the zeroed-out state (see below). `a5hash` functions should not be used for MACs or other strictly cryptographic purposes. | In summary, when used with a secret 64-bit seed and non-exposed outputs, `a5hash()` and `a5hash128()` are practically resistant to blinding multiplication attacks. But this resistance is specific and should not be construed as a complete cryptographic security evaluation.

This conclusion applies only to hash functions that use a 64-bit seed. The 32-bit `a5hash32()` function should not be used in open systems due to 32-bit seeding. | Also note that I've considerably improved `a5hash` documentation and addressed "blinding multiplication" risks. Until there's evidence to the contrary, `a5hash` is secure enough for server-side hashing in open systems.

rows.proof: None; informal 'Algorithm analysis' (v2: 2^-122 chance of blinding-multiplication zero-out; BFast: 2^-64 that 8 bytes do not affect output) for 'general inputs', not adversarial. Issue #3 (orlp, 2026-07-12, 'Seed-independent trivial collisions'): Rust PoC force_collide producing colliding 32-byte inputs for any seed; the PoC as posted targets algorithm v1 (crate 0.5.1, 8 constants), not v0.3, but the identical cancellation transfers to v0.3's 17-32-byte path (independently reproduced by the checker, check-museair/v03_collide.py). Author: 'This is a very serious flaw for hashmap applications. I introduced a bit too much parallelism and lacked mixing of the seeds in pursuit of speed.'; orlp: weak seed derivation is 'sketchy against side-channel information ... I wouldn't be surprised if a seed-recovery attack is possible because of that.' (full sentence, corrected). v2 BFast-64 documented weakness: fixed 8-byte prefix makes bytes 9-16 irrelevant for 9-16 B inputs. '_Until then, it should only be used for local sessions!_' is a pre-1.0 stability note, not a DoS statement (kind corrected).

rows.official_claim_quote:
MurmurHash3 is the current version. It was developed after a few people noticed some minor [flaws](MurmurHash2Flaw) in MurmurHash2. MurmurHash3 is a bit faster than MurmurHash2, and should be darn near bulletproof. It also has a super-speedy 128-bit variant for x64 processors, which is useful when trying to generate unique identifiers for large chunks of data. | (1) - because otherwise you could write code that runs Murmur3 backwards, in effect, and generate as many collisions as you want | Murmur's not a crypto hash, so it won't resist intentionally trying to generate collisions.

That said, its mixing is thorough enough that in general use you should be able to use any subset of the output bits and get uniform distributions.

AES hasher: enc = [k0,k1], sum = [k2,k3], key = enc ^ sum. SMHasher3: 64 replicated as RANDOM_STATE[j] = PI2[j] ^ seed (L49-54), so key = PI2[0]^PI2[2] is seed-independent under SMHasher3 seeding (from_random_state L125-133); flagged FLAG_HASH_XL_SEED; rust-ahash-fb excludes 'Many bad seeds'.

rows.official_claim_quote: AHash is the fastest, DOS resistant hash currently available in Rust. AHash is intended *exclusively* for use in in-memory hashmaps. | AHash's output is of high quality but aHash is **not** a cryptographically secure hash. | AHash is designed to prevent an adversary that does not know the key from being able to create hash collisions or partial collisions. | It is not designed to be. Attempting to use aHash as a secure hash will likely fail to hold up for several reasons: 1. aHash relies on random keys which are assumed to not be observable by an attacker. For a cryptographic hash all inputs can be seen and controlled by the attacker. 2. aHash has not yet gone through peer review, which is a pre-requisite for security critical algorithms. 3. Because aHash uses reduced rounds of AES as opposed to the standard of 10. Things like the SQUARE attack apply to part of the internal state. (These are mitigated by other means to prevent producing collections, but would be a problem in other contexts). 4. Like any cypher based hash, it will show certain statistical deviations from truly random output when comparing a (VERY) large number of hashes. (By definition cyphers have fewer collisions than truly random data.)

rows.official_claim_quote:
When NOT to use it: if you have an opponent.  This is not cryptographic.  Given a message, a resourceful opponent could write a tool that would produce a modified message with the same hash as the original message.  Once such a tool is written, a not-so-resourceful opponent could borrow the tool and do the same thing. | It can produce up to 128-bit results.  Large systems should consider using 128-bit checksums nowadays.  A library with 4 billion documents is expected to have about 1 colliding 64-bit checksum no matter how good the hash is.  Libraries using 128-bit checksums should expect 1 collision once they hit 16 quintillion documents.  (Due to limited hardware, I can only verify SpookyHash is as good as a good 80-bit checksum.  It might be better, I can't tell.) | // Up to 3 bytes/cycle for long messages.  Reasonably fast for short messages.
// All 1 or 2 bit deltas achieve avalanche within 1% bias per output bit.

rows.official_claim_short: 'mathematically proven' almost-universal: Pr[h(m)=h(m')] <= n * 2^-60.2 for distinct inputs of up to n bytes with a random seed; almost pairwise independent (n * 2^-124.2) given 128 bits of seed entropy; 'not a cryptographically secure collision-resistant hash if the attacker can see (or worse, request) hash values'.
rows.official_claim_quote: It is **mathematically proven** to have a statistically low collision rate. When initialized with an independently chosen random seed, for any distinct pair of inputs `m` and `m'` of up to `n` bytes the probability that `h(m) = h(m')` is at most `n * 2^-60.2`. This is known as an almost-universal hash function. In fact PolymurHash has a stronger property: it is almost pairwise independent. For any two distinct inputs `m` and `m'` the probability they hash to the pair of specific 64-bit hash values `(x, y)` is at most `n * 2^-124.2`. | PolymurHash has strong collision guarantees for input chosen independently from its random seed. An interactive attacker however can craft its input based on earlier seen hashes. PolymurHash is **not** a cryptographically secure collision-resistant hash if the attacker can see (or worse, request) hash values at will. This is not a failure of the underlying hash, for example the well-known Poly1305 hash used to secure TLS suffers from the same problem. It solves this by hiding its hash values from attackers by adding an encrypted nonce acting as a one-time-pad.

rows.proof: Yes, a written (not machine-checked) proof, extras/universality-proof.md: injective encoding of the input as a polynomial f_m(k) over GF(2^61-1) (block-Horner, degree <= 14 + n/7), so for m != m' the difference has at most that many roots; k uniform over ~2^57.4 keys and independent of the input gives 'Pr[PH(m) = PH(m')] <= n * 2^-60.2'; the bijective mixer plus independent 64-bit s gives 'Pr[H(m) = x  &&  H(m') = y] <= n * 2^-124.2'. Caveats from the author: no formal verification, only bounds-check.py; 'I've spent quite some time going over the proof myself multiple times, so I am fairly confident it's correct. But I'm not aware of anyone else going over them' (issue #7, 2023-09-02, open); pairwise-independence proof needs 128 seed bits (SMHasher3's 64-bit path formally supports only almost-universality); 'There is no collision bound for a fixed key at all' and no claims across seeds or tweaks (issues #8, #3). For the interactive setting no proof: the mix+s construction 'would likely not hold up to proper cryptanalysis in a standard context', only a belief that seed recovery from side channels 'is difficult'. No attacks in tracker (8 issues; #6 'Polymur32?' and #7 open; last activity issue #5 closed 2024-05-02). The pairwise-independence statements are universality bounds, not PRF claims (kind corrected).

However, the ABI is not finalized'. master 9709e11 (2026-01-11); paper umash.pdf dated 2022-02-23 (initial release 2020-08-24; PH->OH 2020-10-13; fingerprint analysis tightened 2022-02-14). SMHasher3 hashes/umash.cpp vendors upstream 32d3cc7 (2022-09-12; SMHasher3 dc76a9fd 2023-01-29); entries UMASH-64, UMASH-128, UMASH-64.reseed, UMASH-128.reseed.
rows.seed_bits: API: key = struct umash_params of 38 x 64-bit words (2432 bits: two polynomial multipliers mod 2^61-1 plus 34 OH words), from random bytes (umash_params_prepare) or umash_params_derive(64-bit value, 32-byte secret) via Salsa20; NULL secret = literal 'Do not use UMASH VS adversaries.'. Separate per-call 64-bit `seed` 'not associated with any collision bound'. SMHasher3: 64 -- UMASH-64/-128 pass the SMHasher3 seed only as that per-call seed with one global default-derived key; .reseed variants re-derive the full key from the seed (default public secret) and also pass it as seed.
rows.official_claim_short: 'provably avoids parameter-independent collisions': Pr[collision] < ceil(s/4096)*2^-55 for inputs of <= s bytes over random parameters; fingerprint < ceil(s/2^26)^2 * 2^-83 (< 2^-70 up to 5 GiB); bounds do not apply if parameters are inferred; the 64-bit seed 'comes with no guarantee'; not for adversaries with side channels.
rows.official_claim_quote: UMASH provably avoids parameter-independent collisions.  For any two inputs of `s` bytes or fewer, the probability that a randomly parameterised UMASH assigns them the same 64 bit hash value is less than `ceil(s / 4096) 2**-55`. | Combining the two hashes yields a [128-bit fingerprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingerprint_(computing)#Virtual_uniqueness) that collides pairs of `s`-or-fewer-byte inputs with probability less than `ceil(s / 2**26)**2 * 2**-83`; that's less than `2**-70` (`1e-21`) for up to 5 GiB of data. | Randomly generated `param` lead to independent UMASH values and associated worst-case collision bounds; changing the `seed` comes with no guarantee. | UMASH should not be used for cryptographic purposes, especially not against adversaries that can exploit side-channels or adapt to the hashed outputs, but it does provide worst-case pair-wise collision bounds. For any two strings of s bytes or fewer, the probability of them hashing to the same value satisfies ε < ⌈s/4096⌉ · 2^−55, as long as the independently generated key is chosen uniformly at random. However, once a few collisions have been identified (e.g., through a timing side-channel in a hash table), the linearity of the hash function makes it trivial to combine them into exponentially more colliding values.

rows.proof: Yes, a written proof sketch (umash.pdf, 24 pp., rendered from umash_reference.py): short inputs (<= 8 B) via an invertible mixer, ~2^-64; OH block compressor (carry-less PH for all but the last 16-byte chunk plus ENH) 2^-63-almost-universal by three-case analysis; Carter-Wegman polynomial over Z/(2^61-1)Z of degree 2*ceil(s/256), 'conservatively' rounded to ceil(s/4096)*2^-55; fingerprint via a twisted second compressor and independent polynomial, 'ε_fp < ⌈s/2^26⌉^2 · 2^−83'. Expectation over uniformly random input-independent keys; hand analysis, not machine-checked. Self-corrected: pvk.ca 2020-10-31 '1.5x the PH bits for one more CLMUL' (title corrected): 'Turns out the part where I simply asserted a property was slightly off 😉. I had to go back to an older proof with weaker bounds, but that’s not catastrophic' (2020-08 announcement had ceil(s/2048)*2^-56 and ceil(s/2048)^2*2^-112). Acknowledged limits: 'If an attacker can infer the contents of these parameters, the bounds do not apply.'; linearity lets known collisions be combined (paper, blog: 'A sufficiently motivated adversary could use something like that to learn more about the key and deploy an algorithmic denial of service attack.' -- a concession, not a resistance claim; kind corrected); issue #18 (2022, birthday-bound wording: 'I was being aggressive in that statement'); #35 (independent params multiply); #15 (xor-in-ENH rejected as 'very predictable'). No break of the bound reported (14 issues, all closed).

rows.seed_bits: Ideal key of the theorems: W+9 independent uniform GF(2^64) words -- 41 words (2624 bits) for 256-byte blocks, 137 (8768 bits) for 1 KB, 17 (1088 bits) for the untested 64-byte row. Shipped code and SMHasher3 seedfn: one 64-bit seed expanded by splitmix64 into BLOCK_WORDS+9 words (k[], u, y, z, c[0..4], t_in; hashes/chainhash.cpp L943-963), a 2^64-member subfamily 'not covered by the theorems' (Remark 15 (A1)). Injective rows: 3 key words (one chain, 64 bits), 4 (8 lanes, 61 bits), 5 (F_2^89-1, 88 bits), 1 (single key). SMHasher3: 64 (FLAG_HASH_CLMUL_BASED; $.bits = 64).
rows.output_bits: 64 (one GF(2^64) element); F_2^89-1 recurrence row outputs the full 89-bit residue (64-bit truncation collides at 2^-25 for a specific pair)
rows.official_claim_short: Theorem 11: for distinct messages of at most n blocks (p = Sn sub-blocks), Pr[collision] <= (Sn+2)/2^64 -- 3/2^64 (256-byte config) and 4/2^64 (1 KB) up to 256 B, ~2^-52 / 2^-53 at 1 MB; Theorem 12: 5-wise independence conditioned on no level-1/2 collision; proven for the ideal W+9-word key only; 200/200 SMHasher3 in the author's fork; no DoS/PRF claim.
rows.official_claim_quote: Theorem 11 (Collision bound). Fix W, S and n ≥ 1, and put p = Sn. For every two distinct messages m ≠ m′ with n(m), n(m′) ≤ n (equivalently: of at most nB bytes each), Pr_{κ,θ,c,τ}[H_{κ,θ,c,τ}(m) = H_{κ,θ,c,τ}(m′)] ≤ (p+2)/2^64 = (Sn+2)/2^64. | For the 256-byte configuration this reads (⌈ℓ/256⌉ + 2)/2^64 for messages of at most ℓ bytes, and for the 1 KB configuration (2⌈ℓ/1024⌉ + 2)/2^64: 3/2^64 and 4/2^64 for messages of up to 256 bytes, 4098/2^64 ≈ 2^−52 and 2050/2^64 ≈ 2^−53 for messages of up to 1 MB. | The ChainHash bounds (Section J) are proved for a key of W + 9 independent uniform field elements; the implementation timed and tested here expands a 64-bit seed with splitmix64, a 2^64-member subfamily that the theorems do not cover (Remark 15). | (A1) Ideal key. Theorems 11 and 12 are about the family indexed by a uniform (κ, θ, c, τ) ∈ F^{W+9} (8(W + 9) random bytes; 328, 1,096 and 136 bytes for W = 32, 128, 8). The implementation derives (κ, θ, c, τ) from a 64-bit seed with splitmix64; the resulting 2^64-member subfamily is not covered by the theorems (no pseudorandomness assumption is made or needed for the ideal-key statements; cf. the counting argument of [LK16, §2.5]).
rows.claim_source: arXiv:2609.06022v1, Appendix J.2 Theorem 11 and the following sentence, p. 172 (corrected from p. 171; pdftotext lines 8730-8741; LaTeX sections/appendix_chainhash.tex L231-244); Table 2 caption, p. 18 (sections/injective.tex L313-317); Appendix J.9 Remark 15 (A1), p. 185 (appendix_chainhash.tex L1098-1105). https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06022

rows.proof: Yes, full proofs: Appendix J (arXiv v1 pp. 169-186; sections/appendix_chainhash.tex): Lemma 58 CLNH 2^-64-XOR-universal at full 128-bit width; Lemma 59 distinct messages give distinct streams (length XOR handles unequal pair counts); Lemma 60/61 injectivity of the three-key recurrence with explicit pivot decoder + three-variable Schwartz-Zippel, level-2 collision <= (p+1)/2^64; Lemma 62 the degree-5 three-multiplication char-2 circuit is a bijective parametrisation of monic quintics; Lemma 63 finalizer 2^-64; Lemma 64 any fixed bijection of the finalizer input (the integer-add twist) is free; Theorem 11 (collision <= (Sn+2)/2^64); Theorem 12 (5-wise independence given level-1/2 distinctness; a k-wise-independence result, not a PRF claim -- kind corrected, likewise the fork commit title 'Add ChainHash, a provably universal 5-independent 64-bit hash'). Injective rows: Lemma 1 + Schwartz-Zippel give n/|F| (three keys), (n+1)/|F| (two), (3n-1)/|F| (single key); lanes (⌈N/L⌉ + L − 1)/|F| shared triple, ⌈N/L⌉/|F| independent triples (Section 5.10). Verification scripts verify5.py, exh5.c, sanity.py, test_chainhash.cpp T1-T9. Stated limits: ideal key only (A1); code-definition equivalence 'tested, not proved' (A2); twist adequacy for a test suite 'an empirical question, not a theorem'; MUM-fold variant of the plain recurrence port (14.4 B/cycle in v1, 14.1 local) explicitly outside the Schwartz-Zippel guarantee and fails the extended seeded-differential tier (15/2^30); the '2^30 seeds, no collision' statement rests on 2026-09-03 runs of degree-3/degree-7 builds, not the shipped degree-5+twist strided definition; open problem: security of unreduced carryless NH under k-wise independent key expansion ('We found no better attack, but also no proof'). No published attack; no issue tracker.

claims.quote: The core function underlying wyhash and wyrand is the MUM function: MUM (A, B) -> C, where A, B, C are 64-bit unsigned integers [online Method]. As @leo-yuriev pointed out [25], MUM function without xoring mask is vulnerable, as MUM (0, X) =0 for any X which loses entropy. As a solution to this problem, we evolved to the masked-MUM=MUM (A^secret, B^seed). By keeping the mask as secrets or randomized value, masked-MUM cannot be cracked trivially in non-cryptographic applications. However, in rare case (2-64), A^secret=0 or B^seed=0 is still possible. Further protection against such cases is also available at some cost of speed by defining a higher security level and invoke the secure-MUM (A, B) =MUM (A, B) ^A^B. It is obvious that for A=0, secure-MUM (A, B) =B will not lose entropy.
claims.location: Design paper, DISCUSSION section, page 10 ("(2-64)" is the superscript 2^-64 flattened by text extraction)

claims.quote: Our further improvements on MUM is the masked-MUM: MUM (A^secret, B^seed), where secret is a predefined 64-bit integer with 32 bits set and seed is status with a uniform distributed number of 1bits. The masked-MUM can protect the MUM from being zero (Discussion), randomize the distribution of real data and produce an avalanche effect. We observed experimentally that just two rounds of masked-MUM suffice to pass all statistical tests.
claims.location: Design paper, METHOD / Mix Function, page 11

row.proof_offered: No proof and no formal security argument. The only reasoning offered is heuristic: the design paper (p.10) argues that XOR-masking the MUM inputs with the secret and the seed means "masked-MUM cannot be cracked trivially in non-cryptographic applications" and that the residual zero-multiplier event has probability 2^-64 (wyhash.h line 17 says 2^-63 for the CONDOM=2 / "strict" fix); the strict-mode argument is one sentence ("for A=0, secure-MUM (A, B) =B will not lose entropy"). The owner states plainly (issue #15) that wyhash "is designed to be as fast as possible, not for security" and "When being intendly attacked wyhash surely break". All quality claims are empirical (SMHasher, BigCrush, PractRand passes). The "about 62 bits" collision figure is an empirical birthday-test observation credited to flyingmutant/Cyan4973/vigna, not a derived bound. The paper's title itself declares the function non-cryptographic.

(5) #130 "WyRand fails 64-bit 1-dimensional collision tests" by vigna, 2023-03-08, closed 2023-09-30 — owner acknowledges wyhash "fails 64-bit collision test with large number of items" and "we should claim only 62 bit strength" (README Limitations line 45 records this, citing flyingmutant/Cyan4973/vigna; xxHash issue #236). (6) #153 "wyhash32 failed on smhasher3" (2026-02-23) and #154 "[QUESTION] wyhash failed on smhasher3 too" (2026-02-24), both by tankf33der, both OPEN with no owner reply as of 2026-09-17; #154 reports "The algorithm cannot fully pass `smhasher3`, neither `default` nor `extra`." and lists the same Zeroes/Permutation/SeedZeroes failures ("237 / 252 passed" on a newer SMHasher3). No issue documents a seed-recovery or seed-independent multicollision attack on the current v4 with a secret seed; the README's only security statement is "We use dynamic secret to avoid intended attack."
row.notes: (1) Version bookkeeping: the header's "final v4.3" (2026-03-22) differs from v4.2 only by the macro name and an extra w1rand PRNG; the hash function has been unchanged since 2023-10-05, so the SMHasher3 "v4.2" results describe the shipped v4.3 exactly. The last GitHub release object is wyhash_final4 (2023-02-06); 4.1/4.2/4.3 exist only as commits on master. (2) "wyhash.strict" in SMHasher3 = WYHASH_CONDOM 2 (`*A^=lo; *B^=hi;` instead of overwrite), the "blind multiplication" protection; it does not change the failing-test list (still 15/250), only speed. (3) The design paper is an unpublished manuscript hosted in the repo root ("Modern Non-Cryptographic Hash Function and Pseudorandom Number Generator", Wang, Barrios Romero, Lemire, Jin; last upload 2021-03-29); it describes v3-era code (32-byte blocks, `_wyp0..5`), predates final4's seed/secret changes, and offers no collision or security analysis beyond the masked-MUM heuristic quoted above. (4) Structure relevant to attacks: per-block state update is `seed = MUM(w0 ^ secret[1], w1 ^ seed)` (wyhash.h line 130/137) with three parallel lanes for >=48 bytes and a 16-byte tail read at `p+i-16` (overlapping the previous block); the finalizer is `MUM(a^secret[1], b^seed)` then `_wymix(a^secret[0]^len, b^secret[1])`. The secret words are public constants unless make_secret is used; the README recommends `make_secret(time(NULL),_wyp)`. (5) SMHasher3 failures are all in the differential ("XOR of hash pairs") analysis of the Zeroes, Permutation-of-two-blocks, and SeedZeroes keysets, i.e. structured key/seed differences produce structured output differences; direct collision counts in those keysets are normal. rurban's older SMHasher reports no quality problems and lists wyhash among the fastest "without quality problems". (6) Lineage: README line 11 says wyhash "has evolved into rapidhash"; rapidhash's README (Nicoshev) no longer mentions wyhash by name and claims to pass all SMHasher and SMHasher3 tests. (7) Speed context from the raw log: bulk 23.17 GiB/s at 3.5 GHz nominal on the SMHasher3 result host.

row.proof_offered: No. There is no design paper (issue #11, 2024-12-02, asked "no paper to disscus about it?"; the author's reply lists only engineering changes vs wyhash: loop unrolling, xoring len into the seed, a nested-if tail, different read alignment for len<=16). No security argument or keyed-hash claim is made; the author explicitly says "Rapidhash focuses on quality and speed, not security" (issue #10) and "this is a non-cryptographic function, it is not our intent to cover specific attacks" (issue #25).

row.acknowledged_attacks: Two seed-independent (key-free) collision constructions are on the tracker, both closed by the author without a fix and with explicit disclaimers: (1) Issue #10 "Seed independent collision" (N-R-K, 2024-11-23, closed 2024-12-02): "Unlike wyhash, rapidhash accepts only a 64bit seed and the rest are constant. This makes it easy to construct seed independent collisions:" with a C program placing the three default secrets at the end of a 192-byte buffer so that 32 random seeds all give hash 0xFCB620EE4C40064C; proposed fix (derive secrets from seed) rejected: "Rapidhash focuses on quality and speed, not security so for now it will be kept as it is." Reopened in comments 2026-01-10 by hoxxep (Rust port maintainer), who cites CVE-2025-27209 and proposes randomised secrets; author reply 2026-01-11: "Random seeds are not recommended to be used." (2) Issue #25 "Trivial collision attack / randomising secrets" (hoxxep, 2025-05-24, closed 2025-05-27): "For inputs of the same length, where `length > 16`, setting `input_bytes[-16..-8] = RAPID_SECRET[1]` will produce the same hash regardless of the other bytes in the input." Author: "this is a non-cryptographic function, it is not our intent to cover specific attacks. Just released V3, which hardens it a bit against this attack." hoxxep's follow-up 2025-05-27: "V3 has simply changed the attack from `a = SECRET[1]` to `a = SECRET[1] ^ length`. All other bytes can change but will result in the same hash." and "`RAPIDHASH_PROTECTED` makes the attack slightly harder, but it still allows for the construction of non-interactive collision attacks unless the seed and secrets are randomised." The v3 code in SMHasher3 (hashes/rapidhash.cpp lines 399-405) confirms the mechanism: tail a = read64(p+i-16) ^ i, then a ^= secrets[1]; b ^= seed; rapid_mum(&a,&b); return rapid_mix(a ^ secrets[7], b ^ secrets[1] ^ i) -- with a == 0 the non-protected product is 0 and the result depends only on the length, not on the seed or the other bytes; the protected variant's xor-accumulating mum keeps b (and hence the seed) in the output for this particular pattern. No CVE or advisory is filed against rapidhash itself; the README does not mention any of this.
row.notes: (1) The project makes NO collision-bound, PRF, or DoS-resistance claim anywhere; its README language is empirical ("pass all tests", "collision probability close to ideal", "Outstanding collision ratio"), and the tracker contains explicit disclaimers. The README never mentions seeds, secrets, RAPIDHASH_PROTECTED, or secret.h; the only seeding statement is that the collision study used "The default seed $0$". Release notes are one-liners ("Rapidhash initial release", "New release, greatly improving hashing throughput", "Re-releasing V3"). (2) SMHasher3's 'rapidhash' entry is the RAPIDHASH_UNROLLED code path (RapidHash64<false,false,true>); 'rapidhash.protected' is the compact path with the xor-accumulating rapid_mum (RapidHash64<false,true,false>). rapidhashMicro/Nano are documented as producing "same output as Rapidhash for inputs up to 80 bytes" / "up to 48 bytes" respectively. (3) The v3 tag was moved on 2025-08-16 (issue #33) because two post-May-27 commits changed micro/nano read ordering; "v3" builds taken before that date can differ for micro/nano. (4) secret.h is wyhash's make_secret (Unlicense): each 64-bit word is built from bytes of popcount 4, must be odd, pairwise XOR popcount exactly 32, and prime; its only comment is "//make your own secret" -- no security statement. The author's stated secret guidance (issue #13) is "generate secrets that recursively have the same amount of bits set to 1 in each half." (5) The header's "Triplet of 64-bit secrets" doc comment is stale for v3 (rapid_secret has 8 entries; indices 0-7 are used). (6) README's "fastest recommended hash function by SMHasher" refers to rurban's table, which tests v1 with a 32-bit verification 0xAF404C4B, not v3. (7) SMHasher3 README lists 31.98 avg cycles for rapidhash.protected while the raw file's Average line prints 31.97 (rounding in the summary script). (8) For context, SMHasher3 also carries the Rust port (hoxxep) under 'rust-rapidhash' (250/250, 35.01 cycles, 8.66 B/c), 'rust-rapidhash.seed' (250/250, 34.93, 8.67), 'rust-rapidhash.p' / '.p.seed' (250/250, 45.47/45.62, 3.02) and '.fast' variants that fail 131-132 tests; these are a separate implementation and not covered here. (9) All 32 issues on the tracker were listed; #10, #13, #17, #25 are the only ones about seeds/secrets/security. (10) Issue-comment quotes were retrieved with the gh CLI on 2026-09-17 and saved verbatim in issue_<n>.md; README/header quotes are from the raw files saved in the scratchpad (pinned commits in SOURCES.md).

row.seed_bits_api: 64-bit seed: XXH3_64bits_withSeed(const void* input, size_t length, XXH64_hash_t seed) and XXH3_128bits_withSeed(..., XXH64_hash_t seed) (xxhash.h L1182, L1425; doc L1163/L1410: "The 64-bit seed to alter the hash result predictably."; L1173: "seed == 0 produces the same results as @ref XXH3_64bits()."). Alternative keying by a "secret" byte string of at least XXH3_SECRET_SIZE_MIN = 136 bytes (xxhash.h L1191), default secret 192 bytes; *_withSecret and *_withSecretandSeed variants; XXH3_generateSecret derives a secret from arbitrary input. Spec §"Seed and Secret" (doc/xxhash_spec.md L367): "The seed is an unsigned 64-bit value, and the secret is an array of bytes that is at least 136 bytes in size. The default seed is 0". L388: "The seed and the secret cannot be specified simultaneously (`*_withSecretAndSeed` is actually `*_withSeed` for short and medium inputs <= 240 bytes, and `*_withSecret` for large inputs)." For inputs > 240 bytes with a seed, the secret used is defaultSecret with derivedSecret[2i] += seed, derivedSecret[2i+1] -= seed (spec L392-398); for <= 240 bytes the seed enters directly alongside the default secret.
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64 bits. SMHasher3's seed_t is uint64_t (platform/seedt_variant1.h) or uintptr_t (seedt_variant2.h), both 64-bit on the x86-64 result host; the wrappers pass it whole: hashes/xxhash.cpp L1449-1450 "static void XXH3_64( const void * in, const size_t len, const seed_t seed, void * out ) { uint64_t h = XXH3_64bits_withSeed<bswap>(in, len, seed);" and L1461-1462 likewise for XXH3_128bits_withSeed. The raw logs confirm "64-bit seeds" in every Seed test line. XXH3-64 additionally has $.seedfixfn = excludeBadseeds with a 30-entry $.badseeds list (L1618-1626; comment L1616-1617: "Seems to be simpler-than-expected relationship between seed and hash for keys of 1-3 bytes."); XXH3-128 has no bad-seed list. SMHasher3 also registers XXH3-64/128 ".reinit" and ".regen" variants where the 64-bit seed is expanded into the 192-byte secret (xxh3_initsecret / xxh3_generatesecret) and the hash is then called with seed 0 via *_withSecretandSeed.
row.output_bits: 64 (XXH3_64bits, XXH64_hash_t) and 128 (XXH3_128bits / XXH128, XXH128_hash_t struct {low64, high64}). SMHasher3 $.bits = 64 (XXH3-64, verification_LE 0x1AAEE62C) and 128 (XXH3-128, verification_LE 0x288DAA94). Note: the low 64 bits of XXH128 equal XXH3-64 only for "large" inputs (> 240 bytes) — maintainer in issue #1016 (2025-03-03): "From what I remember, the equality happens for \"large\" data only."

row.proof_offered: No. Neither the README, xxhash.h, the specification (doc/xxhash_spec.md), the blog post nor the wiki offers a proof, a universality/almost-universality bound, a PRF/MAC reduction, or any quantified adversarial collision bound. The evidence offered is empirical: passing SMHasher and rurban's fork (README L13-14, L81-83), the author's own brute-force collision counter ("massive collision tester", README L85-88) with the wiki table showing counts in line with the birthday bound (XXH3: 314 collisions vs 312.5 expected for 100 Gi hashes of 256 B; XXH128: 0), and informal probability remarks in comments: xxhash.h L4721-4723 "This only has a 1 in 2^63 chance of 8 consecutive bytes cancelling out" (about the known multiply-by-zero multicollisions for 17-240 B), and issue #261 "It translates into a `1 / 2^64` chance for this to happen accidentally". The maintainer explicitly declines adversarial guarantees: spec L40 "is not meant to avoid intentional collisions"; issue #175 "a non-cryptographic hash should not even try to \"resist\" an attack"; issue #180 "should a non-cryptographic hash offer a guarantee of zero seed-independent collision ? I thought the definition of non-cryptographic implies there is no such guarantee." The only security-flavoured statements are comparative and unquantified: a secret "makes it more difficult for an external actor to prepare an intentional collision" (xxhash.h L1209) and _withSecret gives "a higher level of protection than 64-bit seed" (L1854-1855).

row.acknowledged_attacks: The project acknowledges, in its own code and issue tracker, that XXH3 has seed-independent / seed-dependent structured collisions and offers no adversarial guarantee: (1) Issue #180 "Simple collisions in XXH3" (NoHatCoder, 2019-03-16, pre-release xxh3 branch): "The seed is in most cases not applied properly, so it is easy to fabricate generic collisions that work regardless of the seed. It also does nothing to protect the input data. Seed and input is easily recoverable from hashes on small input." easyaspi314 demonstrated "1099511627776 collisions" (5-8 byte inputs) and "18446744073709551615 collisions" (16-byte inputs) for any seed; Cyan4973 replied "Note that xxHash being non cryptographic, it's not supposed to offer any protection in this space." and then changed the short-length kernels (2019-03-17: "secret keys are xored, instead of added. This makes it more difficult to reason about delta between keys."). (2) Issue #261 "Collisions in mid-range keys" (easyaspi314, 2019-09-30): multiply-by-zero in XXH3_mix16B lets inputs matching the (default) secret cancel 16-byte blocks; Cyan4973: "Are we back to this discussion that an attacker knowing the secret key can manufacture a collision ? `xxhash` being _non-cryptographic_, it is not designed to protect from such case." and "It translates into a `1 / 2^64` chance for this to happen accidentally". Mitigation adopted for v0.7.4 ("using different parts of the secret on the short hashes" — "Sure ! It looks like a good mitigation idea.", 2020-02-11). The residual issue is documented in shipped code: xxhash.h v0.8.3 L4707-4708 "DISCLAIMER: There are known *seed-dependent* multicollisions here due to multiplication by zero, affecting hashes of lengths 17 to 240." (3) Issue #344 (gzm55, 2020-03-24): XXH3 and XXH128 fail demerphq/smhasher's seed-avalanche test for lengths 0-3; Cyan4973 "I confirm the test results for `len` within `[0-3]`." — "Improved in v0.7.4". (4) Issue #1016 (2025): XXH128.low64 == XXH3-64 is "best effort", holds only for inputs > 240 bytes. (5) Not (yet) acknowledged: issue #1127 "XXH3 (64- and 128-bit): a fixed pair of 32-240-byte messages collides with probability about 2^-27 over a uniformly random seed or secret", opened 2026-09-02 by thomasahle (the present author), still open with 0 comments as of 2026-09-17. No maintainer statement about hash-flooding/DoS exists anywhere in the sources reviewed.
row.notes: (1) Official position in one line: xxHash calls itself "non-cryptographic" everywhere (xxhash.h L39, xxhash.com title, spec L40) and the spec says it "is not meant to avoid intentional collisions"; the only positive claims are statistical (SMHasher pass, "Quality 10", birthday-paradox collision counts) plus the unquantified "makes it more difficult for an external actor to prepare an intentional collision" for custom secrets. No document mentions DoS, hash flooding, or PRF/MAC security; the string "DoS" does not occur in README, xxhash.h, the spec, or the blog post. (2) The README's SMHasher claim ("All variants successfully complete the SMHasher test suite") refers to Appleby's original SMHasher and rurban's fork; on SMHasher3 (a much larger 250-test suite with 64-bit seed tests) XXH3-64 fails 27 and XXH3-128 fails 36 tests, mostly seed-related (SeedZeroes, SeedSparse, SeedBlockLen, SeedBlockOffset, SeedBIC) plus BIC/Sparse/PerlinNoise/Bitflip. rurban's own table also flags xxh3 with "DiffDist bit 7 w. 36 bits, BIC". (3) Seeding structure relevant to a random-secret attack model: for inputs <= 240 bytes the 64-bit seed is combined with the fixed 192-byte default secret inside the mixers (spec: *_withSecretandSeed is "actually `*_withSeed` for short and medium inputs"); for > 240 bytes the secret is defaultSecret with alternate 64-bit words += seed / -= seed. XXH3-64's 17-240 byte path uses XXH3_mix16B, whose multiply-by-zero multicollisions the code itself documents ("1 in 2^63" per 8-byte cancellation event); the maintainer's stated accidental-collision estimate is 1/2^64 per event (issue #261). (4) SMHasher3-specific caveats: XXH3-64 runs with 30 excluded bad seeds; the ".reinit"/".regen" variants (seed expanded into the secret via XXH3_initCustomSecret / a generateSecret-like routine, then hashed with seed 0) are SMHasher3 constructions, not upstream API entry points, and .reinit fails Sanity. (5) xxhash.com (and xxhash.h) additionally list AVX2 speeds "__XXH3__ (AVX2) | 64 | 59.4 GB/s | 133.1 | 10" and "__XXH128__ (AVX2) | 128 | 57.9 GB/s | 118.1 | 10" (Intel i7-9700K); the README v0.8.3 table lists the SSE2 rows quoted above. (6) The WebFetch summarizer refused to return the README verbatim, so all upstream files were downloaded raw with curl at tag v0.8.3 and quoted from the saved copies; line numbers in the claims refer to those files and match GitHub's blob line numbers. Multi-line comment quotes have the " * " prefix stripped and soft line breaks joined with a single space; nothing else was altered. (7) Issue #1127 (2^-27 seeded collision pair, 32-240 B, both widths) is the present author's own report and has no maintainer reply yet; it should be presented in the post as "reported, unanswered", not as acknowledged. (8) XXH128 low64 == XXH3-64 for inputs > 240 B (maintainer, #1016), so for long inputs the low half of XXH128 offers exactly XXH3-64's behaviour.

row.seed_bits_api: 64-bit seed: `static _MUM_INLINE uint64_t mum_hash (const void *key, size_t len, uint64_t seed)` (mum.h L390; doc comment L388-389: "Hash data KEY of length LEN and SEED. The hash depends on the target endianess and the unroll factor."). The seed is consumed only as `seed + len` (L392 `_mum_hash_aligned (seed + len, key, len)`; L331 `result = seed + len;`), then `result = _mum (result, _mum_block_start_prime)` (L228). Also `mum_hash_init (uint64_t seed) { return seed; }` (L373) and `mum_hash64 (uint64_t key, uint64_t seed)` (L384). Separately, `mum_hash_randomize (uint64_t seed)` (L356-370, "Set random multiplicators depending on SEED.") calls `srand (seed)` and redraws every multiplication constant (7 named primes + the 16-entry _mum_primes[] table) with `rand () % 256` bytes, i.e. a 64-bit argument feeding libc srand, which on most platforms keeps only 32 bits. Without it the constants are fixed public compile-time values.
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64 bits: every mum3 REGISTER_HASH block has `$.hash_flags = 0` (no FLAG_HASH_SMALL_SEED, so is32BitSeed() is false) and the HashFn receives the full `seed_t seed`; mum_aligned() calls `_mum_hash_aligned<...>(seed + len, in, len)` exactly as upstream (hashes/mum_mir.cpp L187-192). SMHasher3 never calls mum_hash_randomize: the multiplication constants are the fixed upstream values (L69-85 of mum_mir.cpp).
row.output_bits: 64 (`$.bits = 64` for all mum3 entries; upstream mum_hash returns uint64_t; mum_hash64 returns size_t). No 32- or 128-bit variant of MUM V3.

claims.quote:
# **Update (Nov. 28, 2025): Implemented collision attack prevention in VMUM and MUM-V3**
* The attack is described in Issue#18
* The code in question looks like
```
    state ^= _vmum (data[i] ^ _vmum_factors[i], data[i + 1] ^ _vmum_factors[i + 1]));
```
  It is easy to generate data which makes the 1st operand of `_vmum`
  to be zero.  In this case whatever the second operand is, the hash
  will be generated the same.  So an adversary can generate a lot of
  data with the same hash
* This is pretty common code mistake for a few fast hash-functions. At
  least I found the same vulnerability in [wyhash](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash/blob/46cebe9dc4e51f94d0dca287733bc5a94f76a10d/wyhash.h#L130) and [rapidhash](https://github.com/Nicoshev/rapidhash/blob/d60698faa10916879f85b2799bfdc6996b94c2b7/rapidhash.h#L383)
claims.location: README.md, top-of-file update banner, raw lines 1-12

claims.quote:
* After the code change, the safe variants of VMUM and MUM hashes are
  switched on by default.  If you want previous variants, please use
  macros VMUM_V1 and MUM_V3 correspondingly.  I believe there are still
  cases when they can be used, e.g. for hash tables in compilers.
* The fix consist of checking _vmum operands on zero and use nonzero value instead
  * all checks are implemented to avoid branch instruction generations to keep hash calculation pipeline going
  * still the checks increase length of critical paths of calculation
  * in most cases, new versions of VMUM and MUM generates the same hashes as the previous versions
* The fix results in slowing down hash speeds by about **10%** according to my benchmarks

row.proof_offered: No. There is no design paper and no collision-probability bound anywhere; the only security text is heuristic: the README asserts preimage "resistance" from brute-forcing `lo(x*C)+hi(x*C)` ("probably requires `2^63` tries") and that with randomized constants preimages "probably will be close to finding two or more solutions of *Diophantine* equations"; the blog post says "It is difficult to find a different operand that produces the same hash" and offers a puzzle instead of an argument. The author explicitly disclaims analysis: "nobody made a differential crypto-analysis of mum-hash. I am not going to do this." (issue #9, 2018) and, for MUM512, "No differential cryptanalysis has been performed, nor have the probabilities of various attacks on the hash function been investigated." Collision resistance is never claimed; the 2025-11-28 README update concedes a seed-independent multicollision in V3 ("an adversary can generate a lot of data with the same hash").

row.acknowledged_attacks: 1) Issue #18 (orlp, 2025-11-25, closed 2025-11-28): "Trivial seed-independent multicollisions against VMUM" - a fixed 8-byte prefix makes every 16-byte key hash identically regardless of seed, because `data[i] ^ factor[i] == 0` zeroes the multiplication and erases `data[i+1]`. The author's README update explicitly extends this to MUM-V3 ("Implemented collision attack prevention in VMUM and MUM-V3 ... So an adversary can generate a lot of data with the same hash") and notes "I found the same vulnerability in wyhash and rapidhash". Fix: commit 52c7d6ce (2025-11-28, message "Fixing issue #8 (hash collision attack prevention)." - sic, refers to #18) adds `_mum_xor` returning `b` when `a ^ b == 0`; the old behaviour remains available as MUM_V3, and SMHasher3's mum3 is that old behaviour. In MUM V3 the vulnerable pairwise loop only runs while `len > _MUM_UNROLL_FACTOR * 8` (64 bytes at the x86-64 default, 16 bytes for SMHasher3's unroll1), so the seed-independent multicollision needs keys longer than one unroll block; word i set to `_mum_primes[i]` frees the 64-bit word i+1 (inference from the code, not stated by the project). 2) Issue #9 (2018): the author states no cryptanalysis exists and only brute-force preimage (2^64) was considered. 3) Third-party: SMHasher3 badseeddesc "All seeds collide on keys of all 0x00 versus all 0xFF for some lengths (e.g. 32 bytes, 80 bytes)" and (inexact) "All seeds give zero hashes on keys of all zero bytes if len+seed==0"; rurban: "too many bad seeds", PerlinNoise failure; README itself: "It fails on Perlin noise and bad seeds tests". No CVE; no other issues discuss security (full issue list saved in issues_list.txt).
row.notes: (1) Which "MUM v3" the post is about matters: upstream flipped its default on 2025-11-28. SMHasher3's mum3.* (SRC_FROZEN) equals the pre-fix MUM_V3, and the project's own README now says that variant lets "an adversary ... generate a lot of data with the same hash" while still endorsing it "e.g. for hash tables in compilers". The post-fix default has no name in the code; the README benchmark tables call it "MUM-V4". (2) The README's headline "passes **all** SMHasher tests" is about Appleby's original SMHasher; the same README concedes rurban failures (Perlin noise, bad seeds), and SMHasher3 fails it on 25-36 of 250 tests (exact) or 98-132 (inexact). The MUM_QUALITY build that the README says passes rurban is not in SMHasher3. (3) Choice of representative SMHasher3 entry: mum3.exact.unroll3 is the upstream x86-64 default (aarch64 default is unroll4; PPC64 unroll3); mum3.exact.unroll1 scores best (25 failures) but is a 16-byte-block configuration nobody ships. The unroll power changes hash values, not just speed. (4) Seed handling: the seed enters only as `seed + len` before the first multiply, so (seed, len) pairs with equal sum start from identical state; this is the plausible mechanism behind the SeedBlockLen/SeedBlockOffset failures and the SMHasher3 badseeddesc (inference, not a project statement). (5) The security section's numbers ("2^63 tries", "2^64 solutions", "Diophantine equations") concern preimages of one multiply step, never collisions or seed recovery; no epsilon, no universality, no PRF claim. mum_hash_randomize's "randomly chosen multiplication constants" go through libc srand/rand, so the effective randomness is at most rand()'s state (32 bits on glibc), not 64. (6) Author's blog (2025-11-25, same day issue #18 was filed) frames DoS resistance as a design criterion ("weak hash functions open the door to denial-of-service attacks") and claims "good strength" for MUM-based hashes, again without argument. (7) rurban's README table has MUMv3 at 16628 MiB/s, 21.58 cycles/hash with verdict "PerlinNoise, too many bad seeds, machine-specific (32/64 differs)"; rurban's "MUM" row (the older version) says "UB, too many bad seeds". (8) All quotes above were copied from the saved raw files in the scratchpad (README/mum.h line numbers refer to those files at the pinned commits); the WebFetch summary of the blog was cross-checked against the saved text before quoting.

claims.quote: Note that `komihash` is not cryptographically secure. In open systems and internal server-side data structures, it should be used only with a secret seed to minimize the risk of collision attacks (hash flooding). However, using the default seed (0) reduces overhead by 1-2 cycles/hash (depending on the compiler).
claims.location: README.md, section "Introduction", lines 42-46 (as fetched 2026-09-17 from raw.githubusercontent.com/avaneev/komihash/main/README.md)

claims.quote: It is worth noting that `komihash` uses, at its core, a simple mathematical construct and contains no arbitrarily chosen or artificially tuned constants. The base state of the function consists of the first few digits of the fractional part of pi, and this state can be replaced with any uniformly distributed random values. This means that the statistical properties (collision resistance) of `komihash` are based not on manual fine-tuning but rather on its mathematical construct.
claims.location: README.md, section "Introduction", lines 34-40

claims.quote: The function passes all [SMHasher](https://github.com/rurban/smhasher) and [SMHasher3](https://gitlab.com/fwojcik/smhasher3/-/tree/main/results) tests. The function was also tested with the [xxHash collision tester](https://github.com/Cyan4973/xxHash/tree/dev/tests/collisions) under various settings, and the collision statistics met expectations.
claims.location: README.md, section "Introduction", lines 48-51

claims.quote: Another important difference between `komihash` and these functions is that it parses the input message without overlap. While overlaps allow a function to use fewer branches, they are considered "non-ideal" because they potentially cause collisions and seed-value flaws. In addition, `komihash` features superior seed-value handling and Perlin noise hashing support.
claims.location: README.md, section "Introduction", lines 28-32

claims.quote: Another reason is that for a non-cryptographic hash function, this step provides no additional security. While it may seem to protect against simple "state-XOR" collision attacks, in practice it offers no protection given the power of [SAT solvers](https://github.com/pysathq/pysat). In less than a second, a SAT solver can forge a preimage that produces the required hash value. It is also important to note that in fast hash functions such as `komihash`, the input message completely determines the state variables and the result.
claims.location: README.md, section "Discussion", lines 316-323

claims.quote: Here, $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are 64-bit portions of the message or string being hashed. Since $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$ are uniformly distributed values, such mixing is equivalent to mixing the message with a cryptographic one-time pad (bitwise addition modulo 2). The message's statistical distribution is irrelevant and does not affect the uniform distribution of $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$.
claims.location: README.md, section "KOMIRAND", lines 388-393 (same argument as code comment komihash.h lines 835-838: "The following XOR operations are equivalent to mixing the message with a cryptographic one-time pad (bitwise addition modulo 2). The message's statistics and distribution are thus unimportant.")

claims.quote: a reliable 64-bit hash can accommodate 2.1 billion diverse binary objects (e.g., files in a file system or entries in a hash map) with a low probability of collisions.
claims.location: README.md, section "Discussion", lines 328-330

claims.quote: It is often desirable to set a specific random seed statically and then use it with the hash function throughout the program's execution. This has the benefit of improving hashing throughput without compromising hash quality.
claims.location: README.md, section "Pre-seeding", lines 81-83

claims.quote: @param UseSeed Optional value to use instead of the default seed. To use the default seed, set this value to 0. This value can have any number of significant bits and any statistical quality. It may need endianness correction if shared between big- and little-endian systems.
claims.location: komihash.h v5.34, doc comment of komihash(), lines 1009-1012

row.proof_offered: No. No design paper exists; the README is the only design document. It gives an informal argument only: collision resistance is said to rest on the "mathematical construct" (multiply-accumulate of the full 128-bit product, no tuned constants) and on the XOR of message words with "uniformly distributed" state being "equivalent to mixing the message with a cryptographic one-time pad". No universal-hashing / epsilon-almost-universal bound, no PRF claim, and no collision-probability theorem is stated. The README explicitly disclaims cryptographic security, says a SAT solver forges a preimage "in less than a second", and says "the input message completely determines the state variables and the result"; the only DoS advice is to use a secret seed to "minimize the risk of collision attacks (hash flooding)". Quality evidence offered is empirical: SMHasher, SMHasher3, xxHash collision tester, PractRand (for komirand).

row.notes: (1) Version mismatch to flag in the post: upstream is 5.34 (2026-08-04) but SMHasher3 upstream results test v5.27 and rurban tests 5.26; per the upstream changelog framing the 5.28-5.34 changes are portability/endianness fixes, but I did not diff the core round, so state the tested version explicitly. (2) Seed structure worth mentioning: the 64-bit seed is not mixed as a whole; the even bits (mask 0x5555...) go into Seed1 and the odd bits (mask 0xAAAA...) into Seed5, each XORed onto a pi-derived constant, then one seedless multiply round (KOMIHASH_HASHROUND, "Required for PerlinNoise") runs before any message is absorbed. The README's "collision resistance" wording (line 39) is explicitly about statistical properties, not adversarial resistance, and the author states the SAT-solver preimage forgery himself. (3) The README's rounding of the SMHasher3 numbers differs from the raw file by 0.01 (32.62 vs 32.63 cycles; 6.24 vs 6.25 bytes/cycle); quote the README row as the headline and the raw lines as the source. (4) The README asserts "passes all SMHasher and SMHasher3 tests", and both trackers agree (SMHasher3 250/250; rurban Quality-problems column empty, verdict GOOD). (5) No design paper; the eBASH/SUPERCOP listing is referenced for speed only. (6) The repo description string on GitHub reads "Very fast, high-quality hash function, discrete-incremental and streamed hashing-capable (non-cryptographic, header-only C/C++) 27GB/s + PRNG". (7) The SMHasher3 tree used is the author's fork checkout (branch mr/seed-differential); the results files and komihash.cpp are byte-identical to upstream/main 3b619371 (no local diff on those paths).

claims.quote: Note that `a5hash` functions are not cryptographically secure. To minimize the risk of a successful collision attack (hash flooding) in open systems and in server-side internal structures, they should only be used with a secret seed, and their output should not be exposed. This is especially important if a malicious party is likely to try to influence the hash outputs. However, if "blinding multiplication" (BM, state cancellation) occurs at a random iteration, these functions immediately recover from the zeroed-out state (see below). `a5hash` functions should not be used for MACs or other strictly cryptographic purposes.
claims.location: README.md, Introduction, lines 34-42 (v5.25/main). The v5.21 README (commit b0ba799, lines 34-41) is identical except that the parenthetical "(BM, state cancellation)" is absent.

claims.quote: `a5hash` hash functions pass all [SMHasher](https://github.com/rurban/smhasher) and [SMHasher3](https://gitlab.com/fwojcik/smhasher3/-/tree/main/results?ref_type=heads) tests. The functions were also tested using the [xxHash collision tester](https://github.com/Cyan4973/xxHash/tree/dev/tests/collisions) at various settings, with collision statistics meeting theoretical expectations.
claims.location: README.md, Introduction, lines 63-68 (main); identical at v5.21 (b0ba799) lines 62-67.

claims.quote: This construction appears to be near the minimal complexity required for high-quality hashing (in the `SMHasher` testing sense).

claims.quote: All `a5hash` functions can be seeded with values of any statistical quality. However, a resistance against hash flooding requires the seeds to be maximum-entropy, uniformly random values.

claims.quote: At the time when this hash function was developed empirically, cryptography had no precise and straightforward techniques for differential cryptanalysis of the multiplication of large independent variables. This complicates a formal proof that the hash function's output and state are uniform.
claims.location: README.md, Design Analysis > Uniformity Analysis, lines 333-336 (main); same text at v5.21 under "## Uniformity Analysis".

claims.quote: At the same time, the empirical evidence is usually sufficient for non-cryptographic contexts, even though it does not constitute hard proof. The following example provides evidence that the `a5hash()` function - specifically, its core operation, the `a5rand()` function - retains practically a uniformly random output on every iteration.
claims.location: README.md, Design Analysis > Uniformity Analysis, lines 350-355 (main).

claims.quote: Although the state variables are approximately uniform, a bit-independence test between the hash function's randomly chosen `UseSeed` parameter and the subsequent `Seed1` and `Seed2` (after multiplication) reveals that up to 6 bits in either state variable can be predicted by the `UseSeed`. At the same time, a differential analysis indicates that the average bit difference (avalanche effect) between the `UseSeed`/`Seed1` and `UseSeed`/`Seed2` pairs is approximately 50% (+/- 0.3%). However, since the `UseSeed` is unknown, this imperfect bit independence only reveals an imperfect dispersion resulting from the multiplication of independent variables, which is to be expected.
claims.location: README.md, Design Analysis > State Uniformity Margin, lines 443-451 (main).

claims.quote: Another observation, unrelated to the `UseSeed` biases, is a perfect correlation in the 63rd bits of both `Seed1` and `Seed2` after the initial multiplication involving the hash function's known constants. This correlation reduces the effective entropy of both state variables at the initial iteration - and of `val01` and `val10` constants throughout - by 1 bit relative to the theoretical 64-bit entropy.
claims.location: README.md, Design Analysis > State Uniformity Margin, lines 453-458 (main).

claims.quote: BM should not be confused with the Birthday Paradox problem. Statistically, BM is a problem concerning the equality of an arbitrary input and an independent, uniformly distributed value, which has a theoretical probability of `2^-64` for 64-bit variables.
claims.location: README.md, Design Analysis > Blinding Multiplication, lines 474-477 (main).

claims.quote: Given that the `a5hash` state is unbiased and approximates an expected random collision statistics for two of its variables (`Seed1` and `Seed2`) at all times (minus a 1- to 4-bit entropy margin, as detailed in the "State Uniformity Margin" chapter), BM is triggered in either variable with a theoretical probability of `2^-62` (optimistic) or `2^-59` (pessimistic) for a 64-bit secret seed. In either case, this probability can be considered negligible for non-cryptographic use cases.
claims.location: README.md, Design Analysis > Blinding Multiplication, lines 505-511 (main).

claims.quote: When the `UseSeed` is unknown, and when the output of the hash function is unknown (as in the case of server-side structures), it is impossible for an attacker to know immediately whether BM was triggered in any of the hash function iterations: collision confirmation requires a statistically-significant timing information, thus needing hash collisions to accumulate quickly to be measurable.
claims.location: README.md, Design Analysis > Blinding Multiplication, lines 513-518 (main).

claims.quote:
In summary, when used with a secret 64-bit seed and non-exposed outputs, `a5hash()` and `a5hash128()` are practically resistant to blinding multiplication attacks. But this resistance is specific and should not be construed as a complete cryptographic security evaluation.

This conclusion applies only to hash functions that use a 64-bit seed. The 32-bit `a5hash32()` function should not be used in open systems due to 32-bit seeding.
claims.location: README.md, Design Analysis > Blinding Multiplication, lines 530-537 (main, v5.25).

This conclusion applies only to hash functions that use a 64-bit seed. The 32-bit `a5hash32()` function should not be used in open systems due to security concerns.

row.proof_offered: No proof and no formal security argument. The README states outright that a formal uniformity proof is out of reach ("This complicates a formal proof that the hash function's output and state are uniform") and that its evidence "does not constitute hard proof"; the function is described as "developed empirically". What is offered is empirical: PractRand runs on the a5rand core fed sparse structured inputs (Uniformity Analysis), a count_indep() bit-independence estimate on the 0xAAAA/0x5555 constants (Why A5?), a measured UseSeed-to-state bit-independence/avalanche test (up to 6 predictable bits; perfect bit-63 correlation; 1-4 bits of entropy margin), and a heuristic per-iteration blinding-multiplication probability of 2^-62 (optimistic) to 2^-59 (pessimistic) for a secret 64-bit seed, plus a timing-noise cost argument (a 64-fold input increase example). No universality/collision-probability theorem, no PRF claim, and the author explicitly disclaims cryptographic security and MAC use.

row.notes: (1) Version drift: SMHasher3 tests v5.21 (commit b0ba799), upstream main is v5.25, rurban tests v5.13; the README quotes above are given from both the current README and the v5.21 README where wording differs (the "Seeding" section and the "(BM, state cancellation)" gloss exist only in the newer README; the BM summary changed from "practically secure against the \"blinding multiplication\" attack" to "practically resistant to blinding multiplication attacks", and the a5hash32 caveat from "due to security concerns" to "due to 32-bit seeding"). (2) The README's "pass all SMHasher and SMHasher3 tests" statement is borne out by the SMHasher3 results (250/250 for all four variants) and rurban's empty Quality-problems cell, but rurban's verdict is for v5.13 and covers only the 64-bit function. (3) The README's own benchmark table was produced with SMHasher3 commit 7be7e9e820724779926c052db41c15bf88d5863b on a Xeon E-2386G (README "Comparisons", lines 129-131). (4) Seed mechanics relevant to the adversarial measurement: the seed is consumed by a single 64x64->128 multiply of two pi-derived constants (each XORed with MsgLen) masked by 0xAAAA…/0x5555…; the per-block adders val01/val10 become seed-dependent only when MsgLen > 16 (a5hash.cpp lines 73-76); for MsgLen <= 16 the message is XORed straight into Seed1/Seed2 and two multiplies finalize. Blinding multiplication (an input word equal to the current Seed1 or Seed2, zeroing the product) is the weakness class the author himself analyses. (5) The author's a5hash-32 disclaimer ("should not be used in open systems") is the only variant-specific security statement. (6) The README's 2^-64 / 2^-62 / 2^-59 figures are per-iteration BM-trigger probabilities under a secret uniformly random seed, not collision bounds over the message space; no epsilon-almost-universal or similar bound is stated anywhere. (7) SMHasher3 HashInfo for all four variants carries no $.badseeds/$.seedfix entries and no FLAG_HASH_* beyond ENDIAN_INDEPENDENT (+SMALL_SEED for -32). (8) Web search reliability was intermittent during this run (one WebSearch call returned "unavailable" and was retried); all quotes were taken from raw files downloaded with curl and saved in the scratch directory, not from the search summaries.

row.version: SMHasher3 (local tree) tests MuseAir v0.3 — four registrations, all labeled "MuseAir v0.3": MuseAir (Standard), MuseAir.bfast (BFast), MuseAir-128, MuseAir-128.bfast. Upstream (eternal-io/museair) has since moved the algorithm to v2 (released 2026-07-13), and its own CHANGELOG declares every version at or before v1 (which includes v0.3) "deprecated ... compromised and should no longer be used." The Rust crate is at 0.6.0 (implements algorithm v2). So the version SMHasher3 benchmarks here is one upstream now treats as broken; v2 is NOT in this SMHasher3 tree.

row.seed_bits_api: 64-bit for the 64-bit hash: v0.3 API `fn hash(bytes: &[u8], seed: u64) -> u64` and `fn hash_128(bytes: &[u8], seed: u64) -> u128` — note v0.3's 128-bit function also takes a SINGLE u64 seed. The current v2 API takes two 64-bit seeds for the 128-bit variant: `fn hash(bytes, seed: u64) -> u64` and `fn hash128(bytes, seed_a: u64, seed_b: u64) -> u128` (128 seed bits total). No additional secret/key beyond the seed (README: "relies solely on an initial seed, without any additional secret").
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64-bit. The v0.3 museair.cpp in the SMHasher3 tree defines `MuseAirHash(const void* in, const size_t len, const seed_t seed, void* out)` — a single seed_t is threaded to both 64- and 128-bit variants. seed_t is `uint64_t` (platform/seedt_variant1.h) on 64-bit builds, `uintptr_t` (variant2) otherwise. The HashInfo registration blocks carry no $.seedbits/$.badseeds restriction, so SMHasher3 exercises the full 64-bit seed.
row.output_bits: 64 and 128. SMHasher3 v0.3 registers MuseAir and MuseAir.bfast at $.bits=64, and MuseAir-128 and MuseAir-128.bfast at $.bits=128. Upstream v2 additionally exposes an XOR-folded 32-bit output (hash_folded) and an ADD-folded 64-bit output (hash128_folded); those folded forms are not separate registrations in this SMHasher3 tree.

row.proof_offered: No formal proof and no reduction. The README's "Algorithm analysis" section is an informal design argument. It gives heuristic probabilities — a 2^-122 chance of a blinding-multiplication zero-out for the ring accumulator (v2), and 2^-64 for BFast that "a certain 8 bytes of input will not affect the output" (vs wyhash's 2^-63) — but these are back-of-envelope diffusion arguments, not proofs, and they concern accidental collisions on "universal/general inputs," not adversarial resistance. The stronger v0.3 security claim ("not affected by seed-independent attacks") was empirically disproven by a working proof-of-concept in issue #3. AGENTS-style note: security rests on informal analysis plus passing SMHasher3, not on any stated bound with a proof.

row.acknowledged_attacks: Yes — the project acknowledges a serious break of the version SMHasher3 tests here. (1) Issue #3, "Seed-independent trivial collisions," opened by orlp on 2026-07-12 (https://github.com/eternal-io/museair/issues/3): a working Rust PoC (force_collide) that produces colliding 32-byte inputs independent of the seed, affecting 16-32 byte inputs. Author eternal-io replied: "This is a very serious flaw for hashmap applications. I introduced a bit too much parallelism and lacked mixing of the seeds in pursuit of speed." The fix became algorithm v2, and CHANGELOG.md states all prior versions (v0.3 included) are "deprecated ... compromised and should no longer be used." (2) In the same thread, after adding seed mixing, the author notes it "turned into 'seed-dependent trivial collisions'," and orlp raises a further concern that MuseAir's weak seed derivation is "sketchy against side-channel information ... I wouldn't be surprised if a seed-recovery attack is possible." (3) CHANGELOG also records that algorithm v0.4-rc4's 128-bit variant "had insufficient output diffusion and actually failed the SMHasher3 test suite" (fixed with an extra avalanche step). Issue #2 (amadvance) is only about release timing, not an attack.
row.notes:
CRITICAL VERSION MISMATCH for the blog: the SMHasher3 tree at source/smhasher3-mr-seeddiff tests MuseAir v0.3 (verification values 0xF89F1683 etc.), but upstream has replaced the algorithm with v2 (2026-07-13) precisely to fix the seed-independent trivial-collision break (issue #3). The project's own CHANGELOG marks v0.3 as compromised. So the SMHasher3 "250/250 pass" for MuseAir here reflects a version the author now says should not be used — SMHasher3's statistical suite did not catch the seed-independent collision (it was found by hand by orlp). If you cite the passing SMHasher3 result you should note it is for the deprecated v0.3.

Two variant families x two widths: Standard vs BFast. Author's own caveats even for the intact algorithm: BFast 64-bit has a documented weakness — README (master, 'Variants' details): "for the 64-bit version of MuseAir-BFast, with a fixed seed and inputs of 9-16 bytes, there always exists a fixed 8-byte prefix such that the content of bytes 9-16 does not affect the hash output"; the suggested workaround is the 128-bit BFast ADD-folded to 64-bit.

DoS/randomization posture: MuseAir uses only a public/known-structure seed and no independent secret. README explicitly says this makes it "unsuitable for direct use on servers" and (v0.3) that it "should only be used for local sessions." orlp's issue-#3 discussion recommends a thread-local SECRET for hashmap use; the author declined to add side-channel/seed-recovery protection.

rurban smhasher: MuseAir is NOT listed in rurban/smhasher's README quality/speed table (no 'muse' rows; no doc/MuseAir*.txt), so there is no rurban verdict to cite.

Numbers were measured on the local SMHasher3 tree (3.5 GHz); the project's own README quotes bulk throughput on an AMD Ryzen 7 5700G (v0.3: ~28.5 GiB/s Standard, ~33.3 GiB/s BFast) — different machine, do not conflate with the local cycles/bytes-per-cycle figures.

The local SMHasher3 branch is named 'mr-seeddiff' and its HEAD commit (5309a850, 2026-09-05) adds a 'SeedDifferential test for seeded differential collisions' — a custom test not in upstream SMHasher3; the MuseAir raw results predate it (committed 2025-10-16) and were generated with the standard 250-test suite, so the SeedDifferential test is not reflected in MuseAir's 250/250.

acknowledged_attacks — says issue #3's "working Rust PoC (force_collide) ... produces colliding 32-byte inputs independent of the seed" as if it ran against the v0.3 algorithm SMHasher3 tests. The PoC as posted uses an 8-entry CONSTANT and `wmul(CONSTANT[4] ^ u, CONSTANT[5])` / `wmul(CONSTANT[6] ^ v, CONSTANT[7])`, i.e. algorithm v1 (crate 0.5.1, released 2026-07-11, the day before the issue). v0.3 has 7 constants and `wmul(CONSTANT[2], CONSTANT[3] ^ u)` / `wmul(CONSTANT[4], CONSTANT[5] ^ v)` (SMHasher3 hashes/museair.cpp lines 78-79), so the PoC does not run unmodified on v0.3. The same cancellation DOES transfer to v0.3's 17-32-byte path: reproduced in experiment/claims/check-museair/v03_collide.py (64-bit Standard and BFast, 32-byte inputs, 8 seeds incl. 0, 0xdeadbeef, 2^64-1 and random). Right text: "PoC targets algorithm v1 (crate 0.5.1); the identical cancellation applies to v0.3's len>16 && len<=32 path (verified independently), and CHANGELOG deprecates all pre-v2 versions including v0.3." Also "affecting 16-32 byte inputs" should read 17-32 bytes (the branch is `len > 16`).

row.seed_bits_api: 64 bits for the one-shot API: `T1HA_API uint64_t t1ha2_atonce(const void *data, size_t length, uint64_t seed);` and `T1HA_API uint64_t t1ha2_atonce128(uint64_t *__restrict extra_result, const void *__restrict data, size_t length, uint64_t seed);` (t1ha.h lines 496-504). Internally t1ha2_atonce calls init_ab(&state, seed, length) / init_cd(&state, seed, length), i.e. the second state word is the message length, not extra seed (src/t1ha2.c). The streaming API takes two 64-bit words = 128 seed bits: `T1HA_API void t1ha2_init(t1ha_context_t *ctx, uint64_t seed_x, uint64_t seed_y);` (t1ha.h line 508), with init_ab(&ctx->state, seed_x, seed_y); init_cd(&ctx->state, seed_x, seed_y). Seed injection is affine: a = seed_x, b = seed_y, c = rot64(seed_y,23) + ~seed_x, d = ~seed_y + rot64(seed_x,19).
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64 bits. SMHasher3's seed_t is 64 bits on this host (platform/seedt_variant1.h: `typedef uint64_t seed_t;` / variant2 `typedef uintptr_t seed_t;`). The wrapper hashes/t1ha.cpp lines 1143-1170 does `init_ab(&state, (uint64_t)seed, length); ... init_cd(&state, (uint64_t)seed, length);` exactly mirroring upstream t1ha2_atonce, for both the 64- and 128-bit outputs. The Keyset 'Seed' tests report "64-bit seeds" (e.g. raw line 3059: "Testing   3-byte keys, 64-bit seeds, 1572864 reps"). The .incr variants call `t1ha2_init(&ctx, seed, selftest_seeding ? seed : 0);` (line 1191), i.e. seed_y = 0 in tests; the comment at lines 1182-1185 explains: "t1ha published selftest code uses the seed twice during initialization, while published SMHasher validation codes use it once. Default to once so SMHasher3 tests are consistent, but allow selftests to use published KAT tables."
row.output_bits: 64 (t1ha2_atonce / SMHasher3 t1ha2-64, $.bits = 64, verification LE 0x8F16C948) and 128 (t1ha2_atonce128 / SMHasher3 t1ha2-128, $.bits = 128, verification LE 0xB44C43A1). t1ha.h lines 490-491: "Note: Due performance reason 64- and 128-bit results are completely different each other, i.e. 64-bit result is NOT any part of 128-bit."

row.proof_offered: None. The project offers no collision bound, no PRF/universality claim, no DoS/hash-flooding statement and no security argument for t1ha2. The only strength language is the informal "slightly more attention for quality and strength" / "Great quality of hashing" (README lines 194-202, t1ha.h lines 480-488), and the only evidence offered is empirical: SMHasher via rurban's fork ("the quality and speed of _t1ha_ can be easily checked", README line 344) plus 2016 SMHasher speed tables for t1ha1. The README FAQ gives a design rationale (why t1ha does not use NH-style paired multiplication, to avoid "blinding multiplication"/entropy loss) but this is not a proof. Both README (line 58) and t1ha.h (line 35) explicitly disclaim cryptographic use, and the roadmap reserves "Cryptographic" for unreleased t1ha5/6/7.

row.acknowledged_attacks: None for t1ha2. (1) erthink/t1ha issue tracker (GitHub mirror, archived 2025-12-10): the search "is:issue security OR collision OR attack OR seed OR DoS" returns "No results"; the full list via `gh api repos/erthink/t1ha/issues?state=all` is 9 issues (#3 Travis; #16 [Devel] Port to e2k; #25 export `t1ha0_resolve`...; #35 FreeBSD compile fix; #36 "Notes about t1ha_v3 design"; #40 typo; #41 ARM64 AES-NI; #43 "ARM64 AES acceleration?"; #46 Kotlin README) — none is a security or collision report. Caveat: the README says the GitHub copy was restored "from some kind of incomplete backup", so older issues may be missing, and the GitFlic origin exposes no issue list. (2) The project's own docs acknowledge one weakness, for t1ha1 not t1ha2 (README lines 182-187): "Unfortunatelly, [Yves Orton](https://github.com/demerphq/smhasher) discovered that `t1ha1()` family fails the strict avalanche criteria in some cases. ... However, nowadays this issue has resolved in the next `t1ha2()` function"; the same is in SMHasher3 hashes/t1ha.cpp lines 633-638 ("Unfortunately this approach fails the \"strict avalanche criteria\", see test results at https://github.com/demerphq/smhasher."). (3) rurban/smhasher issue #54 "I break t1ha using practrand" (wangyi-fudan, opened 2019-03-11, closed 2019-03-19): "in this way, t1ha is forced to act as a PRNG using his weak seed. And practrand crushed the original t1ha and t1ha1_le. However, t1ha2_atonce seems to survive." — t1ha2 is explicitly not broken there. (4) Web search 2026-09-17 for seed-independent collisions / hash flooding / key recovery on t1ha2: nothing published found.
row.notes: (1) No design paper exists; the README and t1ha.h comments are the only design documentation, and there is no ChangeLog file on GitHub master (404). (2) The project makes NO collision-probability, PRF, universality or DoS/hash-flooding claim for t1ha2 anywhere; the strongest wording is "slightly more attention for quality and strength" and "Great quality of hashing". The word "seed" is never discussed in a security sense; the README's only seed-related security remark is about a competitor ("wyhash ... can lose entropy ... when data could be correlated with the `seed ^ _wypN` values"). (3) The SMHasher pass guarantee in the README ("However, guaranteed that it passes all SMHasher tests.") is written for t1ha0 and predates SMHasher3; in SMHasher3 t1ha0 fails 18/250 and t1ha2-64 fails 3/250 (SeedBlockOffset 0-2, tens of thousands of full 64-bit collisions from 2-bit seeds combined with 2-bit 4-byte blocks), t1ha2-128 fails 1/250 (Avalanche at 40-byte keys). (4) Both SMHasher3 t1ha2 variants use a 64-bit seed with seed_y := message length, exactly as upstream t1ha2_atonce; the 128-bit streaming API t1ha2_init(seed_x, seed_y) is the only way to inject 128 seed bits, and SMHasher3's .incr variants set seed_y = 0. (5) rurban's README simultaneously tags t1ha2_atonce with "Zeroes low3" and lists it among "the fastest hash functions on x86_64 without quality problems"; its doc file header rates it "GOOD". (6) Provenance caveats for the checker: GitHub erthink/t1ha is an archived mirror rebuilt from an incomplete backup (README's own words) and shows only 9 issues; the GitFlic origin has no releases/tags and the "5.0.0 / 2026-09-16" string on gitflic.ru is the platform footer. (7) The README 'Scores' tables are explicitly "obtained in 2016" and list 't1ha' (then t1ha1) at 35.55 cycles/hash and 12228.80 MiB/s; they are not t1ha2 measurements. (8) The 2016-2020 copyright header and identical t1ha.h across master/v2.1.4/GitFlic mean 'v2.1.4' and 'T1HA_VERSION 2.1.1' describe the same code; SMHasher3's embedded copy (web.archive.org snapshot of 2021-12-09) is that code, converted to C++ templates ("Performance and hash results should match the original code.", hashes/t1ha.cpp line 55).

row.version: v1.1.1 (June 17, 2013, per upstream NEWS; last release). SMHasher3 hashes/cityhash.cpp line 2: "CityHash family v1.1.1, by Geoff Pike and Jyrki Alakuijala". Upstream repo github.com/google/cityhash is unchanged in substance since 2013 (SMHasher3 marks the family SRC_FROZEN); the 64-bit functions have been unchanged since v1.1 (Oct 22, 2012), and NEWS says v1.1.1 made "No changes to any of the functions, unless you had been using CityHash32()".
