row.seed_bits_api: Upstream city.h exposes three 64-bit entry points: `uint64 CityHash64(const char *buf, size_t len)` (no seed); `uint64 CityHash64WithSeed(const char *buf, size_t len, uint64 seed)` (one 64-bit seed); `uint64 CityHash64WithSeeds(const char *buf, size_t len, uint64 seed0, uint64 seed1)` (two 64-bit seeds = 128 bits). Header comment (city.h lines 80-81): "Hash function for a byte array.  For convenience, a 64-bit seed is also hashed into the result." STRUCTURAL NOTE (city.cc lines 404-411): `CityHash64WithSeed(s,len,seed) { return CityHash64WithSeeds(s, len, k2, seed); }` and `CityHash64WithSeeds(s,len,seed0,seed1) { return HashLen16(CityHash64(s, len) - seed0, seed1); }` -- i.e. the seed(s) are NOT mixed into the message processing at all; the unseeded 64-bit hash is computed first and the seed is applied afterwards by a 128->64-bit finalizer (HashLen16 = Hash128to64). For a fixed seed this post-mix is a bijection of the unseeded hash value, so any collision of unseeded CityHash64 is a collision for every seed.
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64 bits. SMHasher3 tests "CityHash-64" as CityHash64WithSeed with the framework's seed_t (platform/seedt_variant1.h: `typedef uint64_t seed_t;`, variant2: `typedef uintptr_t seed_t;` -- both 64-bit on the x86-64 results host) passed straight through: hashes/cityhash.cpp lines 673-678: `City64(...) { h = CityHash64WithSeed<bswap>((const uint8_t *)in, len, (uint64_t)seed); PUT_U64<bswap>(h, out, 0); }`. HashInfo (lines 773-787): desc "Google CityHash64WithSeed", hash_flags = 0 (no FLAG_HASH_NO_SEED / SMALL_SEED / XL_SEED), impl_flags FLAG_IMPL_MULTIPLY_64_64 | FLAG_IMPL_ROTATE | FLAG_IMPL_LICENSE_MIT, bits = 64, verification_LE = 0x5FABC5C5, verification_BE = 0x355FC63A. SMHasher3's WithSeeds path is only reachable with seed0 = k2 (constant), so the second 64-bit seed is not exercised. (Upstream's own README note: "SMHasher is designed to pass a 32-bit seed ... For our functions that accept a seed, we use the given seed directly (padded with zeroes)".)
row.output_bits: 64 (CityHash64 / CityHash64WithSeed / CityHash64WithSeeds). The family also has CityHash32 (32), CityHash128/CityHashCrc128 (128) and CityHashCrc256 (256); SMHasher3 "CityHash-64" is the 64-bit output only.

claims.quote:
CityHash provides hash functions for strings.  The functions mix the
input bits thoroughly but are not suitable for cryptography.  See
"Hash Quality," below, for details on how CityHash was tested and so on.
claims.location: README, section "Introduction", lines 7-9 (saved as upstream_README)

claims.quote:
CityHash is intended to be fast, under the constraint that it hash very
well.
claims.location: README, section "Performance on long strings: 64-bit CPUs", lines 40-41

claims.quote:
We like to test hash functions with SMHasher, among other things.
SMHasher isn't perfect, but it seems to find almost any significant flaw.
SMHasher is available at http://code.google.com/p/smhasher/

SMHasher is designed to pass a 32-bit seed to the hash functions it tests.
No CityHash function is designed to work that way, so we adapt as follows:
For our functions that accept a seed, we use the given seed directly (padded
with zeroes); for our functions that don't accept a seed, we hash the
concatenation of the given seed and the input string.

The CityHash functions have the following flaws according to SMHasher:

(1) CityHash64: none

(2) CityHash64WithSeed: none
claims.location: README, section "Hash Quality", lines 152-166

may have gone slightly overboard in trying to please SMHasher and other
similar tests, but we don't want anyone to choose a different hash function
because of some minor issue reported by a quality test.

claims.quote: We’re pleased to announce the new CityHash family of hash functions for strings. We’re releasing two functions today: CityHash64 and CityHash128. They hash strings to 64- and 128-bit hash codes, respectively. These functions aren’t suitable for cryptography, but our experience so far shows that they’re great for, say, hash tables.

row.proof_offered: None. No collision bound, PRF/keyed-hash claim, or DoS-resistance claim is made anywhere in the README, NEWS, city.h/city.cc comments, or the 2011 announcement. The only quality evidence offered is empirical: passing Appleby's SMHasher (README "Hash Quality": "(2) CityHash64WithSeed: none" flaws) and "as far as we know, these functions' statistical properties are sound" (blog). Security is explicitly disclaimed ("not suitable for cryptography", README line 8, city.h line 47, blog paragraph 1). The seed is described only as "For convenience ... hashed into the result" (city.h lines 80-81); nothing is said about seed secrecy, randomization or hash-flooding. The one structural property claimed ("the hash of a+b" is not "easily derived from the hashes of a and b", city.h lines 58-60) is stated without argument and does not concern collisions.

row.acknowledged_attacks: The project itself never acknowledges any attack: NEWS and README contain no mention of CVE, attacks, hash-flooding or security (grep of both files: zero hits). The only project-tracker entry is google/cityhash issue #10 "CVE-2012-6051" (auto-migrated from code.google.com; originally reported by Al3xBio on 3 Dec 2012, migrated 2015-08-14, closed the same day by the migration with 0 comments and no maintainer reply): body quotes MITRE, "Google CityHash computes hash values without properly restricting the ability to trigger hash collisions predictably, which allows context-dependent attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) via crafted input to an application that maintains a hash table, as demonstrated by a universal multicollision attack." and asks "Given that the NEWS file does not mention this, is v1.1.0 affected?" -- never answered. NVD CVE-2012-6051 (published 2012-11-28) carries the same description; its references are the ASFWS 2012 slides by Aumasson and Bosslet and the cityhash NEWS file. Published attacks (external): (1) Aumasson, Bernstein, Bosslet, "Hash-flooding DoS reloaded: attacks and defenses", 29C3, 2012-12-29 (abstract, fahrplan.events.ccc.de/congress/2012/Fahrplan/events/5152.en.html): "We show that it's not enough, at least for systems relying on \"MurmurHash\" or on Google's \"CityHash64\", by presenting powerful \"universal multicollision\" attacks for those functions." Slides (aumasson.jp/siphash/siphashdos_29c3_slides.pdf) state "CityHash is weaker than MurmurHash" and list 16 distinct 16-byte strings all with CityHash64(...) = b553de6f34e878f; take-home slide: "CityHash and Python's hash are weak too…". (2) Orson Peters, "Breaking CityHash64, MurmurHash2/3, wyhash, and more...", orlp.net, 2024-11-02, section "Breaking CityHash64": a constant-time pre-image for 32-byte inputs to the libc++ CityHash64 variant: "Note that d is only used once, in the final expression. This makes it a prime target for attacking the hash. We will choose a, b and c arbitrarily, and then solve for d to compute a desired hash outcome." and "The chance that a random uint64_t forms 8 printable ASCII bytes is (94/256)^8 ≈ 0.033%. Not great, but cityhash64_preimage32 is so fast that having to repeat it on average ~3000 times to get a purely ASCII result isn't so bad." with ten printable strings (e.g. "orlp-cityhash64-D-:K5yx*zkgaaaaa") that "all hash to 1337 using CityHash64". Because CityHash64WithSeed = HashLen16(CityHash64(s,len) - k2, seed), any such unseeded collision holds for every seed.
row.notes: (1) Key structural fact for the blog's "worst-case resistance" column: in CityHash64WithSeed the seed never touches the message; it is applied afterwards as HashLen16(CityHash64(s,len) - k2, seed), a bijection of the unseeded value for each fixed seed. Hence every unseeded collision (Aumasson/Bosslet 2012 multicollisions, Peters 2024 pre-images) is a collision for all 2^64 seeds, and the 45 SMHasher3 failures are all in the Seed* test families (no keyset test fails). SMHasher3 only exercises 64 of the 128 possible WithSeeds bits (seed0 is fixed to k2). (2) Version: the numbers in SMHasher3 are for v1.1.1 (hashes/cityhash.cpp line 2); the 64-bit functions have been unchanged since v1.1 (2012-10-22). Beware that "CityHash64" in the wild has variants: libc++'s std::hash uses an older CityHash64 (Peters attacked that variant; the 17-32-byte path he shows uses k3, a constant that v1.1's city.cc no longer has), and Abseil/FarmHash carry descendants; the SMHasher3 CityHash-64 verification value 0x5FABC5C5 identifies the exact function. (3) Upstream README "Hash Quality" claims of "none" SMHasher flaws refer to Appleby's original SMHasher (32-bit seed); rurban's smhasher reports "Sparse, TwoBytes" for City64, and SMHasher3 reports 45/250 failures, so the README's flaw list is outdated relative to modern test suites. (4) Google Code issue #10 (CVE-2012-6051) got no maintainer response; the NEWS file for v1.1.1 (June 2013) does not mention the CVE. (5) The results README lists CityHash-64 in the "Failing hashes" table; the raw file has no embedded version stamp -- the release attribution (20251015-release-5035a923) is inferred from the commit date of ea0b94f9 (2025-10-16) versus the README footer's three listed versions. (6) The 2011 blog text uses typographic apostrophes ("aren’t", "functions’"); quotes above preserve them.

row.seed_bits_api: 64 bits: uint64_t Hash64WithSeed(const char* s, size_t len, uint64_t seed). A two-seed form Hash64WithSeeds(s, len, uint64_t seed0, uint64_t seed1) takes 128 bits. In farmhashna the seed never enters the compression loop; it is folded in after the unseeded hash: Hash64WithSeeds(s,len,seed0,seed1) = HashLen16(Hash64(s, len) - seed0, seed1), and Hash64WithSeed(s,len,seed) = Hash64WithSeeds(s, len, k2, seed) (src/farmhash.cc lines 579-585). The unseeded Hash64 uses the fixed constant "const uint64_t seed = 81;". The public farmhash::Hash64WithSeed dispatches to farmhashna::Hash64WithSeed on every platform (src/farmhash.cc line 1930).

claims.quote: FarmHash provides hash functions for strings and other data.  The functions mix the input bits thoroughly but are not suitable for cryptography.  See "Hash Quality," below, for details on how FarmHash was tested and so on.
claims.location: README.md, section "Introduction", lines 11-13

claims.quote: We like to test hash functions with SMHasher, among other things. SMHasher isn't perfect, but it seems to find almost any significant flaw.
claims.location: README.md, section "Hash Quality", lines 136-137

claims.quote: SMHasher is designed to pass a 32-bit seed to the hash functions it tests. For our functions that accept a seed, we use the given seed directly (padded with zeroes as needed); for our functions that don't accept a seed, we hash the concatenation of the given seed and the input string.
claims.location: README.md, section "Hash Quality", lines 140-143

claims.quote: Some minor flaws in 32-bit and 64-bit functions are harmless, as we expect the primary use of these functions will be in hash tables.  We may have gone slightly overboard in trying to please SMHasher and other similar tests, but we don't want anyone to choose a different hash function because of some minor issue reported by a quality test.
claims.location: README.md, section "Hash Quality", lines 145-149

claims.quote: This file provides a few functions for hashing strings and other data.  All of them are high-quality functions in the sense that they do well on standard tests such as Austin Appleby's SMHasher. They're also fast.  FarmHash is the successor to CityHash.
claims.location: src/farmhash.h, header comment, lines 26-29

claims.quote: Functions in the FarmHash family are not suitable for cryptography.
claims.location: src/farmhash.h, header comment, line 31

claims.quote: By the way, for some hash functions, given strings a and b, the hash of a+b is easily derived from the hashes of a and b.  This property doesn't hold for any hash functions in this file.
claims.location: src/farmhash.h, header comment, lines 39-41

claims.quote: Hash function for a byte array.  For convenience, a 64-bit seed is also hashed into the result. May change from time to time, may differ on different platforms, may differ depending on NDEBUG. uint64_t Hash64WithSeed(const char* s, size_t len, uint64_t seed);

src/farmhash.cc, namespace farmhashna, lines 579-585 (seed is a post-mix on the unseeded Hash64)

claims.quote:
There are many possible definitions of hash function quality.  For example, one might want a list of keys and their hashes to provide no pattern that would allow an opponent to predict anything about the hashes of other keys.  Although I cannot prove it, I think I can meet this and many other definitions of quality with

  f(s) = SHA-3(concatenation of z and s),

where z is some secret string known only to me.
claims.location: Understanding_Hash_Functions (Geoff Pike, "Version 0.2 --- early draft"), section "1 INTRODUCTION", lines 17-25

claims.quote: Therefore, one should rarely plan to spend much CPU time on a secure hash function (such as SHA-3) or a near-universal hash function (such as VHASH) when seeking the best possible performance from a hash table.  Against that, those types of hash functions can limit the risk of pathological performance problems when one is designing around typical hash-based algorithms that stick with a single hash function no matter how it behaves on the data at hand.
claims.location: Understanding_Hash_Functions, section "3 HASH FUNCTIONS FOR HASH TABLES", lines 141-147

claims.quote: FarmHash was developed with little-endian architectures in mind.  It should work on big-endian too, but less work has gone into optimizing for those platforms.

row.proof_offered: None. The project offers no collision bound, no universality or PRF claim, and no security argument for any FarmHash function. The only quality evidence is empirical: "We like to test hash functions with SMHasher, among other things" (README, Hash Quality). The single structural claim is the non-extendability remark in farmhash.h ("the hash of a+b is easily derived from the hashes of a and b. This property doesn't hold for any hash functions in this file"), stated without justification. The design itself is undocumented: issue #1 "Add documentation on the hash algorithm" (2015-08-14, still open) asks for it; the only reply (rurban, 2016-03-09) says "it's a tiny improvement over CityHash ... an ordinary 3 step hash". Understanding_Hash_Functions explicitly contrasts FarmHash-style table hashes with "a secure hash function (such as SHA-3) or a near-universal hash function (such as VHASH)", i.e. FarmHash is positioned as neither.

row.notes: (1) Structural fact that explains the SMHasher3 result: in farmhashna the seed is applied only as a final post-mix, Hash64WithSeeds = HashLen16(Hash64(s,len) - seed0, seed1) with seed0 fixed to k2 for the one-seed API. Two messages that collide under the unseeded Hash64 therefore collide under every seed, and the seed has no influence on the internal state; the seed only passes through one HashLen16 (a two-multiply 128-to-64 mix). All 45 SMHasher3 failures are in the seed test families (SeedZeroes, SeedSparse, Seed, SeedAvalanche, SeedBIC, SeedBitflip) and the worst seed-avalanche/bitflip bits are the top seed bits 61-63; every input-keyset test passes. rurban's SMHasher, which has weaker 32-bit seed tests, rates the same function GOOD with no quality problems. (3) The project makes no collision, universality, PRF, or DoS claim; the only quality claim is passing SMHasher, and the only security-flavoured sentence is the non-extendability remark in farmhash.h. So "FarmHash64WithSeed" in any wrapper (rurban, absl-style ports) means the NA variant measured here. row.seed_bits_api: 32 bits for all three variants: src/MurmurHash3.h lines 29-33 declare "uint32_t seed" for MurmurHash3_x86_32, MurmurHash3_x86_128 and MurmurHash3_x64_128. In x64_128 the two 64-bit state words are both initialised from the same 32-bit seed (src/MurmurHash3.cpp lines 261-262: "uint64_t h1 = seed; uint64_t h2 = seed;"), so the upper 32 bits of the state start at zero; x86_128 sets h1=h2=h3=h4=seed (lines 156-159). Issues #51 (2017-12-21) and #102 (2023-09-07) asked for a 64-bit seed; neither was acted on.

claims.quote: SMHasher is a test suite designed to test the distribution, collision, and performance properties of non-cryptographic hash functions.
claims.location: README.md line 1 (heading) and line 5; identical text on wiki Home line 1 and 5

claims.quote: The SMHasher suite also includes MurmurHash3, which is the latest version in the series of MurmurHash functions - the new version is faster, more robust, and its variants can produce 32- and 128-bit hash values efficiently on both x86 and x64 platforms.
claims.location: README.md line 7 (also wiki Home line 7)

claims.quote: MurmurHash3 is the current version. It was developed after a few people noticed some minor [flaws](MurmurHash2Flaw) in MurmurHash2. MurmurHash3 is a bit faster than MurmurHash2, and should be darn near bulletproof. It also has a super-speedy 128-bit variant for x64 processors, which is useful when trying to generate unique identifiers for large chunks of data.
claims.location: wiki page MurmurHash, line 6 (last paragraph)

claims.quote: MurmurHash3 is the successor to MurmurHash2. It comes in 3 variants - a 32-bit version that targets low latency for hash table use and two 128-bit versions for generating unique identifiers for large blocks of data, one each for x86 and x64 platforms.
claims.location: wiki page MurmurHash3, section Introduction, line 8 (preceded on line 6 by: "(Note - this information is a bit stale, and refers to an earlier version of Murmur3. I'll rewrite it when I have time.)")

claims.quote: The constants for the finalizers were generated by a simple simulated-annealing algorithm, and both avalanche all bits of `h` to within 0.25% bias.
claims.location: wiki page MurmurHash3, section Details, line 50

claims.quote: The final version is a very conservative design, all things considered - it does enough interesting things to its input that there seems to be no obvious way to induce degenerate behavior.
claims.location: wiki Home, Updates entry dated 2/27/2011, line 98

claims.quote: I'm confident enough in this variant of Murmur3 now that I'm offering a small reward to anyone who can find a keyset that breaks it - if you can programmatically generate a keyset that does _not_ use any of Murmur3's internal constants(1) and that still causes a statistically improbable number of hash collisions, you will receive a $50 gift certificate to Amazon and your code will become a new SMHasher test case.
claims.location: wiki Home, Updates entry dated 2/27/2011, line 100 (refers to Murmur3_x86_32)

claims.quote: (1) - because otherwise you could write code that runs Murmur3 backwards, in effect, and generate as many collisions as you want
claims.location: wiki Home, Updates entry dated 2/27/2011, footnote line 102

claims.quote: Murmur3_x86_64, Murmur3_x64_32, and Murmur3_x64_64 have been removed. If you're doing hash table lookup, use Murmur3_x86_32 - it works well on either platform and has much lower latency than x64_128. If you're generating unique IDs for blobs of data, you should be using at least a 128-bit hash.
claims.location: wiki Home, Updates entry dated 2/27/2011, line 106

claims.quote: All versions now have a strong finalization step. It turned out to be faster to trim unnecessary operations off the tail block and use the strong finalizer than to leave them and weaken the finalizer, so that's what I did.
claims.location: wiki Home, Updates entry dated 4/2/2011, line 70

claims.quote: By itself that's not an issue to be worried about, but it does suggest that it might be possible to generate colliding keys of length N and N-1, where the difference in the intermediate hash values was cancelled out by the difference in lengths.
claims.location: wiki Home, Updates entry dated 4/1/2011, line 80 (about the TwoBytes flaw found in Murmur3a before the final revision)

claims.quote:
Murmur's not a crypto hash, so it won't resist intentionally trying to generate collisions.

That said, its mixing is thorough enough that in general use you should be able to use any subset of the output bits and get uniform distributions.

row.proof_offered: None. No collision bound, universality, PRF or DoS-resistance claim is made anywhere in the README, the wiki, the source comments or the issues. The design rationale is entirely empirical: constants chosen by simulated annealing to reach "within 0.25% bias" avalanche (wiki MurmurHash3 line 50), and passing the author's own SMHasher test suite ("SMHasher contains all the test code that I've used to verify MurmurHash3", wiki Home line 120). The author's own footnote (wiki Home line 102) concedes that a keyset using the internal constants can "run Murmur3 backwards, in effect, and generate as many collisions as you want", and in issue #73 he states "Murmur's not a crypto hash, so it won't resist intentionally trying to generate collisions." In issue #58 (2018-04-10) D. Lemire (not the author) notes "There is no established result regarding a randomized MurmurHash's universality (to my knowledge)" and "MurmurHash was not designed with universality in mind."

row.acknowledged_attacks: The project has no security advisory and the author never posted about the 2012 attack, but it is acknowledged inside the issue tracker: (1) Issue #73 (open, 2019-09-03), comment by Spencer-Doak 2019-09-03T22:23:46Z: "In 2012, some researchers scrutinized MurmurHash 3 as if it was a cryptographically strong hashing algorithm. They were able to \"break\" the hashing algorithm such that they could produce collisions within the output regardless of the seed used. This is noted on [the MurmurHash Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MurmurHash#Vulnerabilities), which cites [a blog post that documents the vulnerability](https://emboss.github.io/blog/2012/12/14/breaking-murmur-hash-flooding-dos-reloaded/)." Author aappleby replied 2019-09-03T23:38:08Z: "Murmur's not a crypto hash, so it won't resist intentionally trying to generate collisions." The cited post (Martin Boßlet, "Breaking Murmur: Hash-flooding DoS reloaded", 2012-12-14, now at https://martinbosslet.dev/en/blog/2012/breaking-murmur-hash-flooding-dos-reloaded/) says of Aumasson and Bernstein's 29C3 work: "Among the most impressive results are completely breaking CityHash64, finding a way to retrieve the secret seed of the hash functions being used in Python 2.7.3 and 3.2.3 and completely breaking MurmurHash 2 and 3. \"Completely breaking\" means they were able to produce arbitrary multicollisions even when the seed was properly randomized." and "In fact, the entire transform of the data being processed is independent of the seed that was chosen. It turns out that we can exploit these facts to trick even a randomized MurmurHash into producing collisions at will." (2) Issue #57 (open, 2018-04-04) "[Flaw/Bug in MurmurHash3_x86_128] Collisions within component hashes for small keys - related to shared seed": for keys under 16 bytes "`h2`, `h3` and `h4` have collisions at a 100% rate" because all four state words are initialised to the same seed (affects x86_128 only; the reporter notes "This doesn't affect MurmurHash3_x64_128"). (3) Issue #104 (closed, 2024-02-29): x86_32 is a bijection on exactly-4-byte keys but "For **variable length** 0..4 bytes long input, there are clearly 0x1010101 collisions." (4) Issue #12 (imported from Google Code, 2012-03-10, closed): "Lots of collisions with triplets of integers". (5) Issues #51 (2017) and #102 (2023): 32-bit seed initialises 64-bit state words in x64_128. (6) The author's own wiki footnote (Home, 2/27/2011, line 102) pre-acknowledges that the function can be run "backwards" to "generate as many collisions as you want".
row.notes: Summary: MurmurHash3 makes no formal collision, universality, PRF or DoS claim. The only strength language is informal ("more robust", "should be darn near bulletproof", "no obvious way to induce degenerate behavior", finalizers "avalanche all bits of h to within 0.25% bias", a $50 bounty for a constant-free colliding keyset), and the project itself twice concedes adversarial collisions are trivial (wiki footnote about running Murmur3 backwards; aappleby in issue #73). There is no design paper; the wiki MurmurHash3 page is self-described as "a bit stale" and "refers to an earlier version of Murmur3". Seed is 32 bits in the API for all variants, and the SMHasher3 Seed* tests run with 32-bit seeds (FLAG_HASH_SMALL_SEED); 16 bad seeds (0..15) are excluded for both 128-bit variants and one (0xfca58b2d) for the 32-bit variant. SMHasher3 verdict: all three variants FAIL, roughly a third of the 250 tests, dominated by Seed*-family tests (SeedBlockLen fails for every block length 8-27/8-39, SeedBIC, SeedBitflip, SeedSparse, SeedZeroes) plus BIC, Sparse, Permutation and PerlinNoise; MurmurHash3-32 also fails Text [FooXXXXBar]. Speed (SMHasher3, @3.5 GHz): 44.83 / 47.59 cycles for 1-32 B and 1.00 / 2.36 bytes/cycle bulk for the 32-bit / x64_128 variants. Bulk figure discrepancy: README says 2.36 for MurmurHash3-128 while the raw file's 'Average' lines read 2.37 (its 'Alignment rnd' line reads 2.36). rurban's table classifies Murmur3A as "UB, 1 bad seed, Moment Chi2 69", Murmur3C as "UB, LongNeighbors, Text, DiffDist" and Murmur3F as "UB" only; none appear in his "without quality problems" list, and his "Known exploits" issue #186 lists Murmur with the Boßlet post. The published attack (Aumasson/Bernstein 29C3 2012 as reported by Boßlet: arbitrary multicollisions for MurmurHash2 and 3 "even when the seed was properly randomized") is acknowledged only through a third-party comment in issue #73, to which the author replied that Murmur "won't resist intentionally trying to generate collisions". The WebFetch of the emboss.github.io URL returned only a redirect; the post was saved from its current home martinbosslet.dev. Nothing was written to the project repository; all excerpts are in the scratchpad claims/murmurhash3/ directory with SOURCES_INDEX.txt mapping each quote to file and line.

row.seed_bits_api: 64-bit signed: `gxhash32/gxhash64/gxhash128(input: &[u8], seed: i64)` (src/gxhash/mod.rs lines 15/32/49), `GxHasher::with_seed(seed: i64)` (src/hasher.rs line 76), `GxBuildHasher::with_seed(seed: i64)` (line 151). The i64 is splat into both 64-bit halves of a 128-bit vector: `create_seed(seed: i64) -> State { _mm_set1_epi64x(seed) }` (src/gxhash/platform/x86.rs lines 22-24), and used only as the round key of a single AESENC applied after the seed-independent compression: `finalize(aes_encrypt(compress_all(input), seed))` (mod.rs line 70). `GxBuildHasher::default()` instead transmutes a std `RandomState::new()` into the 128-bit state (hasher.rs lines 157-168; with the `deterministic` feature it is the constant `u128 = 42`). Issue #78 planned an i64->u64 change 'released in v4' — never shipped.
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64 bits: SMHasher3 `seed_t` is `typedef uint64_t seed_t;` (platform/seedt_variant1.h; build/include/Platform.h line 38); hashes/gxhash.cpp casts `(uint64_t)seed` and splats it with `_mm_set1_epi64x(seed)` (line 204) / two memcpys in the generic path (lines 370-373), matching the Rust `create_seed`. Both `gxhash` and `gxhash_64` are registered without any seedfix/badseed entries.
row.output_bits: 128-bit internal state; API exposes 32, 64 and 128 bits (`gxhash32`, `gxhash64`, `gxhash128`, plus `GxHasher::finish` (u64) / `finish_u128`), all as reinterpretations/truncations of the same 128-bit state (article §4.3: 'GxHash takes a simpler path by reinterpreting our state into a smaller X-bit value'). SMHasher3 tests `gxhash` at 128 bits (verification 0x64A77B47) and `gxhash-64` at 64 bits (lower 64 bits, verification 0x48F84240). rurban's smhasher tests gxhash32 and gxhash64.

claims.quote:
### DOS Resistance
GxHash is a seeded hashing algorithm, meaning that depending on the seed used, it will generate completely different hashes. The default `HasherBuilder` (`GxHasherBuilder::default()`) uses seed randomization, making any `HashMap`/`HashSet` more DOS resistant, as it will make it much more difficult for attackers to be able to predict which hashes may collide without knowing the seed used. This does not mean however that it is completely DOS resistant. This has to be analyzed further.
claims.location: Superseded README wording (commit 8bee61e, the revision issue #83 was filed against; lines 106-107), replaced 2024-11-05 by the current '### Security' text

claims.quote:
### Multicollisions Resistance
GxHash uses a 128-bit internal state. This makes GxHash [a widepipe construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkle%E2%80%93Damg%C3%A5rd_construction#Wide_pipe_construction) when generating hashes of size 64-bit or smaller, which had amongst other properties to be inherently more resistant to multicollision attacks. See [this paper](https://www.iacr.org/archive/crypto2004/31520306/multicollisions.pdf) for more details.

### Cryptographic Properties
GxHash is a non-cryptographic hashing algorithm, thus it is not recommended to use it as a cryptographic algorithm (it is not a replacement for SHA). It has not been assessed if GxHash is preimage resistant and how difficult it is to be reversed.
claims.location: Superseded README wording (commit 8bee61e), lines 109-113; removed 2024-11-05

row.proof_offered: No proof and no quantitative security argument. The paper gives only a structural argument: a 128-bit 'wide-pipe' state ('This makes GxHash more resistant to collisions', §4.1; the old README cited Joux's 2004 multicollisions paper) and a seed 'injected at this finalization stage ... as a key for the first AES round' (§4.3). It explicitly says the compression 'has to be empirical' (§4.2) and lists 'Analyze security properties' as future work (§6.2); the quality section is entirely empirical (SMHasher, collision counts on three datasets). The current README calls the DOS/multicollision resistances 'just basic safeguards'. No collision probability, no PRF/universality statement, no key-recovery bound. Structurally the hash is H(x, s) = Finalize(AESENC(CompressAll(x), splat64(s))) with fixed-key Finalize, so any CompressAll collision is a collision for every seed — exactly what issue #83 demonstrates.

row.acknowledged_attacks: Yes — issue #83, https://github.com/ogxd/gxhash/issues/83, OPEN, opened 2024-06-02 by orlp, title "Hash has arbitrary seed-independent multicollisions, is not DoS resistant". Body: "There are probably other issues as well, but this line is particularly problematic: https://github.com/ogxd/gxhash/blob/8bee61e33d2feb78dc076413d10d66929de2face/src/gxhash/platform/x86.rs#L86 / This is trivial to invert and allows you to create arbitrary seed-independent multicollisions. I would suggest not advertising DoS resistance on this hash at all." with a Rust PoC (two 192-byte strings, one AES round with the zero key) asserting `gxhash::gxhash128(&s0, 0) == gxhash::gxhash128(&s1, 0)` and the same for seed 0xdeadbeef. Maintainer ogxd, 2024-06-02: "Thanks a lot for this analysis @orlp! Let's see if we can improve DoS resistance without compromising performance. I don't know if it can be made 100% proof but I'm sure it can be improved (maybe using the seed in the main construction). / Btw DoS resistance is not advertised (unless I missed something?). See in readme: > This does not mean however that it is completely DOS resistant. This has to be analyzed further." orlp, same day: "I disagree. The way it is worded it sounds like it has *some* DoS resistance when there is none at all. Similarly with multicollision resistance." ogxd, 2024-11-05: "Did not has much time to work on this, so in the meantime I've clarified the DOS resistance part in the readme https://github.com/ogxd/gxhash?tab=readme-ov-file#security". purplesyringa, 2024-12-10: "There's probably a lot more problems with DoS resistance here. The most obvious one, IMO, is https://github.com/ogxd/gxhash/blob/main/src/hasher.rs#L113-L117 / `compress_all` is completely independent from the seed, so a collision in `compress_all` affects all seeds." ogxd, 2024-12-10: "Mixing the seed at the start instead of the end should significantly improve DoS resistance. row.notes: (1) Where the seed enters: H(x,s) = Finalize(AESENC(CompressAll(x), splat64(s))), Finalize = three AES rounds with fixed constants (KEYS) — mod.rs line 70, x86.rs. CompressAll never sees the seed, so every CompressAll collision holds for all seeds (purplesyringa's remark in #83; orlp's PoC). The 64-bit seed is duplicated into both halves of the 128-bit round key. This is consistent with SMHasher3's result that every Seed-family keyset (SeedZeroes, SeedSparse, Seed) fails at every length for both variants. (2) 'Passes all SMHasher tests' (README, paper) refers to rurban/smhasher, where gxhash64 shows no test failures and is rated GOOD with 'oob UB, AES only'; SMHasher3 (a different, seed-aware suite) fails 24-25 of 250. (3) The README's Security wording quoted here is the 2024-11-05 revision; crate 3.5.0 (2025-03-11) already ships it. The older text (commit 8bee61e) claimed 'more DOS resistant' and 'inherently more resistant to multicollision attacks' citing Joux 2004, and admitted 'This has to be analyzed further'. (4) The paper (Nov 2023) describes 'version 1.0.0' of the algorithm (article.tex line 318); the README states outputs may change between major versions, so paper details may not match 3.x exactly — the seed-at-finalization structure is the same in the 3.5.0 code. (5) Output widths are truncations of one 128-bit state ('reinterpreting our state into a smaller X-bit value'), so gxhash-64 collisions imply gxhash-128 low-half collisions; SMHasher3 also reports the full 128-bit collisions for `gxhash`. (6) Out-of-bounds reads: the crate deliberately reads past the buffer (README 'Unsafety', article 'unsafe-read-beyond-of-death'); SMHasher3 flags FLAG_IMPL_READ_PAST_EOB, rurban flags 'oob UB'. Requires AES-NI+SSE2 or ARM AES+NEON; no fallback (README 'Hardware Acceleration'); SMHasher3's port adds a generic AES path. (7) SMHasher3 bulk column vs raw 'Average' line differ (19.56 vs 19.87 for gxhash; 19.14 vs 19.56 for gxhash-64) because summarize.sh reads the second 'Alignment rnd' line; documented in quotes.md. (8) Hashes are stable within a major version and identical with/without the `hybrid` VAES path (README 'Hashes Stability', 'hybrid'). (9) Repo description: 'Unsafely fast hashing algorithm 📈'; ~1.03k stars; 1.29M crates.io downloads; last main commit 2025-05-18. (10) `GxHasher` (the Hasher trait path used by HashMap) hashes differently from gxhash128 on the same bytes (README 'Consistency of Hashes When Using the Hasher Trait'); SMHasher3 tests only the direct gxhash128/64 functions. (11) The crates.io/GitHub API calls and all fetched pages are saved under the scratchpad claims/gxhash/ directory; quotes.md indexes every quote with file+line for re-verification.

row.seed_bits_api: 256 bits maximum: `RandomState::with_seeds(k0: u64, k1: u64, k2: u64, k3: u64)` (src/random_state.rs L308-314; each ki is XORed with a PI2 constant). Also `with_seed(key: usize)` = one usize (64 bits on 64-bit targets) mixed with fixed seeds via `from_keys` (L294-297); `new()` / `generate_with` draw 4 x u64 from the RandomSource (OS getrandom by default). The constructor table in the docs (L212-217): "| `with_seed` | Fixed per process | `u64` + static random number |", "| `with_seeds` | Fixed | `u64` x 4 |". In the AES hasher the four words become enc=[k0,k1] (128 b), sum=[k2,k3] (128 b), key=enc^sum (128 b) (src/aes_hash.rs L71-77); in the fallback: buffer=k1, pad=k0, extra_keys=[k2,k3] (src/fallback_hash.rs L56-60).
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64 bits. `seed_t` is `uint64_t`; the port's seedfn `init_state(seed)` sets `RANDOM_STATE[j] = PI2[j] ^ (uint64_t)seed` for j=0..3 (hashes/rust-ahash.cpp L49-54), i.e. one 64-bit seed is replicated into the 256-bit random state by XOR with four constants. Registered with FLAG_HASH_XL_SEED ("XL_SEED means the hash can take more than 64-bits of seed data", hashes/README.latersteps.md L328) but the harness supplies only 64; seed tests in the raw log say "64-bit seeds". rust-ahash-fb additionally has `$.seedfixfn = excludeBadseeds` with `$.badseeddesc = "Many bad seeds, unsure of details; see rust-ahash.cpp for examples"` (L536-538) and a long badseed list. Same seedfn for all four variants.
row.output_bits: 64 (Rust `Hasher::finish() -> u64`; SMHasher3 `$.bits = 64` for rust-ahash, rust-ahash.noshuf, rust-ahash-fb, rust-ahash-fb.nofold). Internal state 256 bits in the AES path ("256bits of state and 256bits of keys are reduced to 64 total bits", FAQ L18). Verification values: rust-ahash LE 0x3BF4383B / BE 0x1B4F8057; rust-ahash-fb LE 0x53C9F167 / BE 0x0AB24D79.

claims.quote: AHash is the fastest, DOS resistant hash currently available in Rust. AHash is intended *exclusively* for use in in-memory hashmaps.
claims.location: README.md, opening paragraph (raw lines 3-5; rendered text, the raw markdown has links on 'fastest' and 'DOS resistant hash'). Saved: upstream_README.md

claims.quote: AHash's output is of high quality but aHash is **not** a cryptographically secure hash.
claims.location: README.md, opening paragraph, raw line 7 (link on 'high quality' stripped)

claims.quote: Because AHash is a keyed hash, each map will produce completely different hashes, which cannot be predicted without knowing the keys. This prevents DOS attacks where an attacker sends a large number of items whose hashes collide that get used as keys in a hashmap.
claims.location: README.md, section 'Design', raw lines 11-12 (second sentence is a markdown link to the wiki page)

claims.quote: AHash does *not* have a fixed standard for its output. This allows it to improve over time. For example, if any faster algorithm is found, aHash will be updated to incorporate the technique. Similarly, should any flaw in aHash's DOS resistance be found, aHash will be changed to correct the flaw.
claims.location: README.md, section 'Goals and Non-Goals', raw lines 18-20

claims.quote: Additionally, aHash is not intended to be cryptographically secure and should not be used as a MAC, or anywhere which requires a cryptographically secure hash. (In these cases `SHA-3` would be a better choice)
claims.location: README.md, section 'Goals and Non-Goals', raw lines 26-27

claims.quote: This allows for DOS resistance even if there is no random number generator available at runtime (assuming the compiled binary is not public).
claims.location: README.md, section 'Flags', bullet for `compile-time-rng`, raw line 61

claims.quote: AHash passes the full SMHasher test suite.
claims.location: README.md, section 'Hash quality', raw line 79 (link to github.com/rurban/smhasher stripped); followed by 'The code to reproduce the result, and the full output are checked into the repo.'

claims.quote: **AHash passes the full SMHasher test suite** both with and without AES support.
claims.location: compare/readme.md, section 'Quality', raw line 18 (link to rurban/smhasher stripped). Saved: upstream_compare_readme.md

claims.quote: At **over 50GB/s** aHash is the fastest algorithm to pass the full test suite by more than a factor of 2.
claims.location: compare/readme.md, section 'Quality', raw line 21

claims.quote: AHash provides DOS resistance by incorporating random keys into the hash.
claims.location: compare/readme.md, section 'DOS resistance', raw line 32

claims.quote: If neither `std` or `compile-time-rng` flags are enabled aHash will fall back on using the numeric value of memory addresses as a source of randomness. This is somewhat strong if ALSR is turned on (it is by default in Rust) but for some platforms this is not available. As a result this should not be relied on.
claims.location: compare/readme.md, section 'DOS resistance', raw lines 38-40

claims.quote: AHash is designed to prevent an adversary that does not know the key from being able to create hash collisions or partial collisions.
claims.location: FAQ.md, section 'How does aHash prevent DOS attacks', raw line 3 (the sentence is a link to the wiki page). Saved: upstream_FAQ.md

claims.quote: If you are a cryptographer and would like to help review aHash's algorithm, please post a comment here.
claims.location: FAQ.md, section 'How does aHash prevent DOS attacks', raw line 5 ('here' links to issue #11)

claims.quote: aHash obeys the 'strict avalanche criterion': Each bit of input has the potential to flip every bit of the output.
claims.location: FAQ.md, section 'How does aHash prevent DOS attacks', bullet at raw lines 12-13 (Wikipedia link stripped); next bullet (line 14): 'Similarly, each bit in the key can affect every bit in the output.'

claims.quote: The `finish` call at the end of the hash is designed to not expose individual bits of the internal state. For example in the main algorithm 256bits of state and 256bits of keys are reduced to 64 total bits using 3 rounds of AES encryption. Reversing this is more than non-trivial. Most of the information is by definition gone, and any given bit of the internal state is fully diffused across the output.
claims.location: FAQ.md, section 'How does aHash prevent DOS attacks', bullet at raw lines 17-19

claims.quote: It is deliberately difficult to 'chain' collisions. (This has been the major technique used to weaponize attacks on other hash functions)
claims.location: FAQ.md, section 'How does aHash prevent DOS attacks', bullet at raw line 21

claims.quote: It is not designed to be. Attempting to use aHash as a secure hash will likely fail to hold up for several reasons: 1. aHash relies on random keys which are assumed to not be observable by an attacker. For a cryptographic hash all inputs can be seen and controlled by the attacker. 2. aHash has not yet gone through peer review, which is a pre-requisite for security critical algorithms. 3. Because aHash uses reduced rounds of AES as opposed to the standard of 10. Things like the SQUARE attack apply to part of the internal state. (These are mitigated by other means to prevent producing collections, but would be a problem in other contexts). 4. Like any cypher based hash, it will show certain statistical deviations from truly random output when comparing a (VERY) large number of hashes. (By definition cyphers have fewer collisions than truly random data.)
claims.location: FAQ.md, section 'Why isn't aHash cryptographically secure', raw lines 50-58

claims.quote: AHash is a high performance keyed hash function. It quickly provides a high quality hash where the result is not predictable without knowing the Key. AHash works with `HashMap` to hash keys, but without allowing for the possibility that a malicious user can induce a collision.
claims.location: src/lib.rs, crate-level doc comment, lines 1-5 (also the top of https://docs.rs/ahash). Saved: upstream_src_lib.rs

claims.quote: aHash avoids this by always immediately combining the incoming data with something derived from a secret key to prevent this problem.
claims.location: Wiki page 'How aHash is resists DOS attacks', section 'Avoiding reversible premixing', raw line 31 (bold in source). Saved: upstream_wiki_How-aHash-is-resists-DOS-attacks.md

claims.quote: aHash avoids this by having an intermediate state which is significantly larger than its output. So if pairs of inputs are found that produce a collision in the output hash, they cannot be combined to produce additional collisions.
claims.location: Wiki page, section 'Preventing chaining', raw line 41 (bold in source); line 43 continues: 'Ultimately this means that even if collisions can be found for aHash, they will not be easily weaponized.'

claims.quote: There is no location or input that can only effect a single bit or byte of the intermediate state.
claims.location: Wiki page, section 'Differential analysis', raw line 60 (bold in source)

claims.quote: Finally this means for any given combined state in the finalization and 64 bit hash output, there are exactly 2^64 keys in the final step which could have produced that output. Similarly for any given key and hash output there are exactly 2^64 combined states which could have resulted in the output.
claims.location: Wiki page, section 'Differential analysis', last paragraph, raw line 116

claims.quote: Note: If DOS resistance is desired one of these should be a decent quality random number. If 4 high quality random numbers are not cheaply available this method is robust against 0s being passed for one or more of the parameters or the same value being passed for more than one parameter.
claims.location: src/random_state.rs, doc comment on `RandomState::with_seeds`, lines 303-305. Saved: upstream_src_random_state.rs

claims.quote: 3. A static counter that adds the memory address of each [RandomState] created permuted with fixed constants. (Similar to above but with fixed keys) - This is the weakest option. The strength of this heavily depends on whether or not ASLR is enabled. (Rust enables ASLR by default)
claims.location: src/random_state.rs, doc comment on `RandomSource` (randomness-source ranking), lines 129-131

row.proof_offered: No proof and no quantitative bound. There is no collision-probability, universality, or PRF bound stated anywhere (README, FAQ, wiki, docs.rs, source). What is offered is an informal design argument: the wiki page "How aHash is resists DOS attacks" (linked from README, FAQ and compare/readme.md) walks a single-byte differential through the AES round, the byte shuffle, and the 3-round finalization and argues that (a) input is always keyed before mixing, (b) the 256-bit state exceeds the 64-bit output so collisions cannot be chained, and (c) the truncated finalization is not invertible ("This is not feasible to reverse because half of the information is simply missing.", wiki line 112). The project itself states the argument is unreviewed: FAQ line 54 "aHash has not yet gone through peer review, which is a pre-requisite for security critical algorithms."; issue #11 "Review" (opened by the maintainer 2019-07-05, still OPEN) reads "Review of aHash is needed both in implementation and conceptually to ensure that it actually satisfies the properties it is attempting to guarantee." A commenter there (ciphergoth) notes "what you want is a cryptographic property - that an attacker who doesn't know the secret key will find it difficult to create a lot of collisions in the hash table. It would be interesting to try to specify this more precisely." The 2023 key-recovery attack (#163) showed the pre-0.8.4 argument was wrong; the fix was checked only by the attacker: "I can confirm that the changes foil my attack. I spent a few hours staring at the new function and couldn't find a similar attack, but I would like to note that I'm not a professional cryptographer, and that this should not be considered an audit." (orlp, issue #163 comment).

row.acknowledged_attacks: 1) Issue #163 (orlp, opened 2023-08-27, closed 2023-10-23) "Critical vulnerability: complete key recovery of AES-based hash through side-channels": "The AES version of aHash only performs a single round of AES between inputs. This is not sufficient, a single-bit difference only gets amplified once in the SubBytes step, leading to one of 256 possibilities, but nothing further. An attacker can guess this to recover the key byte-by-byte, leading to a complete key recovery in ~4000 tests. Note that the **only** thing an attacker has to see is whether two inputs collide, nothing else. The attack can thus be done entirely through side-channels." Maintainer: "Patches have been released in the from of versions `0.8.4`, `0.7.7`, and `0.4.8`" and vulnerable versions were yanked. Wiki 'Yanked versions' line 5: "Versions `0.4.2 - 0.4.7`, `0.5.0 - 0.5.10`, `0.6.0 - 0.6.3`, `0.7.0 - 0.7.6` and `0.8.0 - 0.8.3` were yanked due to the discovery of an attack where if an attacker could control the contents of a string at least 128 bytes in length and could detect if there was an exact hash collision (Which is plausible via timing if it were precise enough and mitigations such as those in Rust's default HashMap were either not in place or were overwhelmed through brute force) then the attacker could calculate the value of an intermediate key which is used in the hashing of long strings. This in turn would allow them to generate an unlimited number of colliding strings for the target HashMap. If the same map / hasher were used for multiple calls this could form the basis of a practical DoS attack." Attack code (recover_ahash_seed) is posted in the issue. 2) Wiki 'Yanked versions' line 3: "The versions in `0.3.*` that are below `0.3.5` were yanked due to a subtle quality problem which could in theory be used by an adversary with full control over the input to produce a partial collision of the lower 32 bits of the hash by guessing with a 1 in 4096 chance." 3) Issue #146 (2022-11-12) "SMHasher Sparse Test Failure" (rurban suite, 16-bit keys): maintainer "I suspect that the issue is one too few aes rounds is being run, and last input is only half defused"; "Resolved in 0.8.4". 4) Issue #210 (waywardgeek, 2024-02-25, closed 2024-03-03) "RandomState has too many collisions in low order bits when hashing a u64": maintainer "this is indeed specific to the u64 specialized fastpath on nightly ... This specific path was made deliberately fast at the expense of quality"; "To be clear: This is it is not a full hash collision but correlation in the low order bits of the output. Which inputs result in low order bit collisions is key dependent, and it only applies to hashing a single u64. This is suboptimal but don't see it as exploitable."; "Fix published in 0.8.10."; no security advisory issued ("I do not believe this is grounds for issuing a SEC advisory."). 5) Issue #11 "Review" (2019-07-05) remains OPEN: no external cryptographic review has been recorded. Saved: issue_163.txt, issue_163_body.json, issue_210*.{txt,json}, issue_146*, issue_11*, issue_10*, upstream_wiki_Yanked-versions.md.
row.notes: (1) Claim type: aHash makes a qualitative DoS-resistance / keyed-unpredictability claim ("designed to prevent an adversary that does not know the key from being able to create hash collisions or partial collisions"; lib.rs: "without allowing for the possibility that a malicious user can induce a collision") and an explicit non-cryptographic disclaimer; it never states a collision probability, epsilon, or universality class, and offers no proof, only the wiki's differential walk-through. It also reserves the right to change the algorithm ("does *not* have a fixed standard"). (2) "Passes the full SMHasher test suite" refers to rurban's SMHasher (checked-in logs from 2023-10-23, 0 FAIL lines; rurban's table lists ahash64 without quality problems). Under SMHasher3 the AES path (rust-ahash) fails 8/250 (all Sparse/TwoBytes collision-count tests, ratios 1.006x-1.074x over expected) while the fallback (rust-ahash-fb) passes 250/250 and is 2.4x faster on short keys (29.14 vs 69.80 cycles) and 1.8x faster in bulk (4.52 vs 2.51 B/cycle) on the SMHasher3 machine; the AES path's short-key cost in SMHasher3 is dominated by per-call state setup (from_random_state + 3 finalization AES rounds). (3) SMHasher3 seeding caveat, verified in the port source: init_state() writes PI2[j] ^ seed into all four state words with ONE 64-bit seed (rust-ahash.cpp L49-54); the AES hasher then computes key = enc ^ sum = (PI2[0]^seed)^(PI2[2]^seed) = PI2[0]^PI2[2] (L124-133, mirroring aes_hash.rs L71-77), so the 128-bit `key` used in finalization (`aesdec(aesdec(combined, self.key), combined)`, aes_hash.rs L211) and in the large-input sum path (L169) is seed-INDEPENDENT under SMHasher3's seeding, and enc ^ sum cancels the seed generally. The same cancellation occurs in the real API if a caller passes k0==k2 and k1==k3 to with_seeds, despite the doc's "robust against ... the same value being passed for more than one parameter". Any adversarial measurement should seed via the 4 x u64 API (with_seeds with independent random words), not via SMHasher3's seedfn, or it will understate the key entropy. (4) Version bookkeeping: master Cargo.toml reads 0.8.10 while tags/crates.io are at 0.8.12; SMHasher3's port tracks 0.8.10 commit 4b73276 (the 2023-10 #163 fix, which changed the update function "to use decryption rather than encryption", PR #173, is included since it predates 0.8.10). (5) rust-ahash-fb carries an SMHasher3 bad-seed exclusion list ("Many bad seeds, unsure of details"), so its 250/250 is with those seeds excluded by seedfixfn. (6) Platform note from FAQ L113-118: AES path needs AES-NI (x86/x86-64; AArch64 also supported per README `nightly-arm-aes` text); otherwise the multiply-based fallback ("folded multiply", wiki 'AHash fallback algorithm') is used. rurban's README (line 355) separately opines that SipHash-in-hashtables is "pure security theatre"; that is rurban's view, not aHash's.

row.hash: SpookyHash V2 (SMHasher3 names: SpookyHash2-64, SpookyHash2-128; also SpookyHash2-32; rurban names: SpookyV2_64, SpookyV2_128)
row.version: V2 ("SpookyHash V2 (labor day 2012)" on the project page; SpookyV2.h line 10: "August 5 2012: SpookyV2 (different results)"). No later version exists; SMHasher3 marks the family SRC_FROZEN.
row.author: Bob Jenkins (burtleburtle.net). Reference C++ at https://burtleburtle.net/bob/c/SpookyV2.h and SpookyV2.cpp; GitHub mirror https://github.com/bobjen/spookyhash (created 2026-03-28). SMHasher3 port by Frank J. T. Wojcik (hashes/spookyhash.cpp).
row.license: Public domain (page: "SpookyHash is a public domain noncryptographic hash function"; SpookyV2.h line 3: "By Bob Jenkins, public domain"). GitHub repo bobjen/spookyhash is licensed The Unlicense (GitHub API). SMHasher3 flags it FLAG_IMPL_LICENSE_PUBLIC_DOMAIN.
row.seed_bits_api: 128 bits for the native API: Hash128(message, length, uint64 *hash1 /* "in/out: in seed 1, out hash value 1" */, uint64 *hash2 /* "in/out: in seed 2, out hash value 2" */) and Init(uint64 seed1 /* "any 64-bit value will do, including 0" */, uint64 seed2 /* "different seeds produce independent hashes" */) (SpookyV2.h lines 53-57, 88-90; page: "The function allows a 128-bit seed."). Convenience wrappers take less: Hash64(message, length, uint64 seed) sets hash1 = seed and hash2 = seed (64-bit seed duplicated into both words, SpookyV2.h lines 62-70); Hash32(message, length, uint32 seed) sets hash1 = hash2 = (uint64)seed (32-bit seed, lines 75-83).
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64 bits. SMHasher3's wrapper (hashes/spookyhash.cpp, function spookyhash<version,hashlen,bswap>) does "h1 = h2 = (uint64_t)seed;" before calling Hash128, i.e. the 64-bit seed_t is duplicated into both 64-bit seed words, exactly like upstream's Hash64 wrapper. $.hash_flags = 0 (no FLAG_HASH_SMALL_SEED), and the seed tests report "64-bit seeds". Only 64 of the 128 seed bits are ever exercised, and the two seed words are always equal.
row.output_bits: 128 native (two uint64 words); 64 and 32 by truncation ("It can produce 64-bit and 32-bit hash values too, at the same speed, just use the bottom n bits."). SMHasher3 registers SpookyHash2-32 ($.bits = 32), SpookyHash2-64 ($.bits = 64, verification_LE 0x972C4BDC), SpookyHash2-128 ($.bits = 128, verification_LE 0x893CFCBE); the 64-bit variant is the first output word h1.

claims.quote: SpookyHash is a public domain noncryptographic hash function producing well-distributed 128-bit hash values for byte arrays of any length. It can produce 64-bit and 32-bit hash values too, at the same speed, just use the bottom n bits.
claims.location: Project page, opening paragraph (below the h1 'SpookyHash: a 128-bit noncryptographic hash')

claims.quote: When NOT to use it: if you have an opponent.  This is not cryptographic.  Given a message, a resourceful opponent could write a tool that would produce a modified message with the same hash as the original message.  Once such a tool is written, a not-so-resourceful opponent could borrow the tool and do the same thing.
claims.location: Project page, section 'Why use SpookyHash?', fourth bullet

claims.quote: It's good.  It achieves avalanche for 1-bit and 2-bit inputs.  It works for any type of key that can be made to look like an array of bytes, or list of arrays of bytes.  It takes a seed, so it can produce many different independent hashes for the same key.
claims.location: Project page, section 'Why use SpookyHash?', second bullet

claims.quote: It can produce up to 128-bit results.  Large systems should consider using 128-bit checksums nowadays.  A library with 4 billion documents is expected to have about 1 colliding 64-bit checksum no matter how good the hash is.  Libraries using 128-bit checksums should expect 1 collision once they hit 16 quintillion documents.  (Due to limited hardware, I can only verify SpookyHash is as good as a good 80-bit checksum.  It might be better, I can't tell.)
claims.location: Project page, section 'Why use SpookyHash?', third bullet

claims.quote: Both V1 and V2 pass all the tests.
claims.location: Project page, paragraph following the V1/V2 download lists (HTML line 34)

claims.quote: Both the short and long V2 hash were tested by froggy out to 2<sup>80</sup> key pairs. It's source-controlled at https://github.com/bobjen/spookyhash.
claims.location: Project page, end of the V1/V2 comparison paragraph (HTML line 44; '2<sup>80</sup>' renders as 2^80)

claims.quote: My frog test is the most stringent test I have for 64-bit and 128-bit noncryptogrpahic hashes.  It hashes n-byte keys that are all zero except for m bits set, for all possible choices of m bits, and looks for collisions.
claims.location: Project page, design discussion, paragraph beginning 'My frog test' (HTML lines ~141-149)

claims.quote: Ideally you'd test a 128-bit hash by checking 2<sup>128</sup> key-pairs, which should produce about 1 collision if the function is adequately random. That's way beyond my means.  2<sup>72</sup> key-pairs is about the limit of my testing abilities.
claims.location: Project page, same 'My frog test' paragraph (HTML lines 146-148; superscripts render as 2^128 and 2^72)

claims.quote: As always, every input bit has to produce 128 bits of apparent entropy before all those bits could be canceled by other input bits.  (128 bits, because the hash produces a 128-bit result.)  My handwave is that after 12 8-byte inputs, there has been as much input as there is internal state, so anything could be overwritten.  So if a delta appears to produce 128 bits of entropy by 12 8-byte inputs after the delta starts, that's good enough.  I wrote screen.cpp to check for that.
claims.location: Project page, design discussion, paragraph beginning 'Testing a trickle-feed mix was a new problem'

// SpookyHash: a 128-bit noncryptographic hash function

claims.location: SpookyV2.h header comment, lines 2-3

claims.quote:

claims.location: SpookyV2.h header comment, lines 12-13

uint64 seed1,       // any 64-bit value will do, including 0
        uint64 seed2);      // different seeds produce independent hashes

claims.quote: SpookyHash is a fast and thorough 128-bit noncryptographic hash function by Bob Jenkins (me) in 2012. It does not use SIMD instructions, it's just normal 64-bit arithmetic, plus xor barrelshift, allowing a lot of instruction-level parallelism.

Comment above SpookyHash::Mix (identical text in SMHasher3 hashes/spookyhash.cpp lines 78-80)

row.proof_offered: No. There is no security proof, no universality/PRF argument, and no adversarial model; the author states the opposite ("This is not cryptographic. Given a message, a resourceful opponent could write a tool that would produce a modified message with the same hash"). What is offered is empirical: avalanche measurements for 1- and 2-bit deltas ("within 1% bias per output bit"), the screen.cpp entropy-expansion check described as "My handwave is that after 12 8-byte inputs, there has been as much input as there is internal state", and the "frog test" collision search over sparse keys (page states V2 "tested by froggy out to 2^80 key pairs" in one place and "2^72 key-pairs is about the limit of my testing abilities" in another; the collision-bound bullet says "I can only verify SpookyHash is as good as a good 80-bit checksum"). All claims are for non-adversarial inputs.

row.acknowledged_attacks: None specific. The project pre-emptively disclaims adversarial use on its own page ("When NOT to use it: if you have an opponent. This is not cryptographic. Given a message, a resourceful opponent could write a tool that would produce a modified message with the same hash as the original message.") but names no concrete attack. The GitHub repo bobjen/spookyhash (created 2026-03-28) has no issues at all; its only item is PR #1 (2026-04-13, "Introduce Easier Compilation Support for C++ via CMake"). No security discussion exists there. External check: the Aumasson/Bernstein/Bosslet 29C3 "Hash-flooding DoS reloaded" slides (saved, text-extracted) do not mention Spooky at all (they attack MurmurHash2/3, CityHash64, Python); the 2012 HN thread on Haberman's "Myths about Hash Tables" (news.ycombinator.com/item?id=4600355) mentions Spooky only in passing ("I don't think that City, Spooky, or Murmur are nearly this linear."). rurban's smhasher lists Spooky V1 with "UB" (misaligned reads) only, and SpookyV2_64/SpookyV2_128 with an empty "Quality problems" column and "GOOD" in doc/SpookyV2_64.txt / doc/SpookyV2_128.txt (zero FAIL lines).
row.notes: (1) Claim framing for the blog: SpookyHash makes NO adversarial/PRF/DoS claim; the only collision statement is the birthday-style expectation for 128-bit checksums on honest inputs ("expect 1 collision once they hit 16 quintillion documents") qualified by "I can only verify SpookyHash is as good as a good 80-bit checksum". (2) The page is internally inconsistent about the frog-test coverage: "tested by froggy out to 2^80 key pairs" (V2 paragraph) vs "2^72 key-pairs is about the limit of my testing abilities" (frog-test paragraph); quote both. (3) Seed model matters for the adversarial column: the API nominally takes 128 seed bits, but the standard Hash64 wrapper and SMHasher3 both duplicate one 64-bit value into both seed words, so the effective secret is 64 bits with the two state words always equal. (4) Structure: messages under 192 bytes (sc_bufSize) go through Short() (4 x 64-bit state a,b,c,d with a=seed1, b=seed2, c=d=0xdeadbeefdeadbeef; ShortMix per 32 bytes, length folded as d += length<<56; ShortEnd finalizer); longer messages use the 12-word trickle-feed Mix with 96-byte blocks and End() = three EndPartial passes. Only add/xor/rotate; no multiplication. (5) SMHasher3 failures are all bit-independence/seed-bitflip statistical biases on very short keys (3-15 bytes), i.e. in the Short() path; the 32-bit truncation passes all 250 tests. SMHasher3 flags: FLAG_IMPL_ROTATE | FLAG_IMPL_LICENSE_PUBLIC_DOMAIN, hash_flags 0, no badseeds listed. (6) rurban smhasher (master README, AMD Ryzen 5 3350G table): SpookyV2_64 13401.13 MiB/sec, 56.18 cycl./hash, 246.33 (11) cycl./map, size 2069, quality column empty; SpookyV2_128 12252.64 MiB/sec, 58.94, 235.46 (2), 2069, empty; Spooky32 (V1) is on rurban's list "the fastest hash functions on x86_64 without quality problems" while V1 rows carry "UB" for misaligned reads. (7) WebSearch surfaced third-party marketing pages (e.g. ssojet.com) asserting SpookyHash "prioritizes collision resistance"; those are not project statements and were not used. (8) The V2 change vs V1 per the page: "In the short hash, there was a d = length that should have been d += length, which means some entropy got dropped on the floor." and removal of the extra mix() before end(); "These changes are not backwards compatible".

claims.quote: HighwayHash, a 5x faster SIMD hash with [security claims](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.06257)
claims.location: README, opening bullet list, lines 5-6 of raw README.md

claims.quote: This package provides two 'strong' (well-distributed and unpredictable) hash functions: a faster version of SipHash, and an even faster algorithm we call HighwayHash.
claims.location: README, section 'Introduction', lines 66-68

claims.quote: To avoid bias, it is important that the hash function be unpredictable and indistinguishable from a uniform random generator. We have verified the bit distribution and avalanche properties of SipHash and HighwayHash.
claims.location: README, section 'Applications', lines 89-92

claims.quote: 64-bit hashes are also useful for authenticating short-lived messages such as network/RPC packets. This requires that the hash function withstand differential, length extension and other attacks. We have published a formal security analysis for HighwayHash. New cryptanalysis tools may still need to be developed for further analysis.
claims.location: README, section 'Applications', lines 94-98

claims.quote: We have devised a new way of mixing inputs with SIMD multiply and permute instructions. The multiplications are 32x32 -> 64 bits and therefore infeasible to reverse.
claims.location: README, section 'HighwayHash', lines 125-127

claims.quote: By contrast, 'strong' hashes such as SipHash or HighwayHash require infeasible attacker effort to find a hash collision (an expected 2^32 guesses of `m` per the birthday paradox) or recover the seed (2^63 requests). These security claims assume the seed is secret.
claims.location: README, section 'Defending against hash flooding', lines 262-266

claims.quote: These guarantee worst-case `log n` bounds for all operations, but only if the hash function is 'indistinguishable from random' (uniformly distributed regardless of the input distribution), which is claimed for SipHash and HighwayHash but certainly not for weak hashes.
claims.location: README, section 'Defending against hash flooding', lines 337-340

claims.quote: In summary, a strong hash function is not, by itself, sufficient to protect a chained hash table from flooding attacks. However, strong hash functions are important parts of two schemes for preventing denial of service.
claims.location: README, section 'Defending against hash flooding', lines 347-349
highwayhash/highwayhash.h, comment above HighwayHashT, lines 87-89
highwayhash/hh_types.h, lines 31-33

claims.quote: HighwayHash is a new pseudo-random function based on SIMD multiply and permute instructions for thorough and fast hashing. It is 5.2 times as fast as SipHash for 1 KiB inputs. An open-source implementation is available under a permissive license. We discuss design choices and provide statistical analysis, speed measurements and preliminary cryptanalysis. Assuming it withstands further analysis, strengthened variants may also substantially accelerate file checksums and stream ciphers.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, Abstract, page 1

claims.quote: We are mainly interested in generating random numbers and message authentication, for which 64-bit hashes are sufficient. These are not ‘collision-resistant’ because adversaries willing to spend considerable CPU time could find a collision after hashing about sqrt(pi/2 * 2^64) inputs. However, small hashes decrease transmission overhead and are suitable for authenticating short-lived messages such as network/RPC packets. If needed, our approach can generate up to 256 hash bits at no extra cost.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, Section 1 Introduction, pages 1-2 (the radical is typeset; pdftotext renders it as 'q ... π2 264')

claims.quote: Section 6 describes our test suite and shows that HighwayHash resists common attack techniques from the literature. Further study may require new cryptanalysis techniques.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, Section 1 Introduction, page 2

claims.quote: HighwayHash can produce up to 256-bit hashes at no additional cost; they also pass our test suite. However, our analysis of differential attacks in Section 6.2 only applies to the 64-bit case. HighwayHash needs further strengthening and analysis before it can serve as a cryptographically secure message digest.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, Section 4.3 (finalization/output size), page 6

claims.quote: We assume 256 key bits are reasonable and sufficient. Attackers have an astronomically low, 1 in 2^(256−s) chance of guessing the key after evaluating 2^s inputs.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, Section 4.4 Initialization, page 6

claims.quote: We are not experienced cryptographers, and do not see a way to reduce the HighwayHash algorithm to provably secure constructions. This multiply-permute scheme may require new methods of cryptanalysis. In the absence of a formal proof, we rely on statistical testing to validate our main claim: HighwayHash is a keyed hash that is indistinguishable from a uniformly random source, with an avalanche effect comparable to a cryptographically random number generator.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, Section 6 Security Analysis (opening paragraph), page 11

claims.quote: In addition to empirical verification, we discuss several possible attacks and whether they apply to HighwayHash. Our attack model assumes that the secret key is initially unknown.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, end of Section 6.1, page 12

claims.quote: The combined probability that both changes from A and B do not affect either mul value is at most 1 in 2^64, so that approach also fails.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, Section 6.2 Differential Attack, page 13

claims.quote: Length extension attacks are infeasible because the calls to PermuteAndUpdate during finalization differ from previous calls to Update.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, Section 6.3 Length Extension Attacks, page 13

claims.quote: To the best of our (non-expert) ability, we have analyzed the algorithm and found no weaknesses. Statistical tests indicate the HighwayHash output bits are as uniformly distributed as the cryptographically secure RDRAND generator. We also considered powerful attacks, including differential and rotational, and are confident the algorithm will withstand these specific attacks. We welcome further cryptanalysis – the family of hash functions built from multiplications and byte permutations had not been studied yet. Assuming this construction remains unbroken, it appears useful for pseudo-random number generators and fast message authentication codes.
claims.location: arXiv:1612.06257v3, Section 7 Conclusion, page 15

claims.quote: FYI we have studied differential/length extension/rotational/SAT solver attacks against HighwayHash without finding a weakness (paper pending publication).
claims.location: Issue #28 'False security claims', comment by jan-wassenberg, 2016-11-25T15:10:45Z

row.proof_offered: No proof. The paper states this explicitly (§6, p.11): "We are not experienced cryptographers, and do not see a way to reduce the HighwayHash algorithm to provably secure constructions. ... In the absence of a formal proof, we rely on statistical testing to validate our main claim". What is offered instead: (a) a strengthened smhasher avalanche test (49 trials, 30M iterations, 4-32 byte inputs, bias compared against Intel RDRAND, §6.1, pp.11-12); (b) informal, attack-by-attack arguments: a hand analysis of two-block differentials giving heuristic probabilities 2^-32 / "at most 1 in 2^64" (§6.2, pp.12-13), an argument that length extension is infeasible because finalization uses PermuteAndUpdate (§6.3), an entropy-loss remark that Update is a permutation (§6.4), a rotational-attack estimate ("1 in 4^1024 bias", §6.5), and an expectation of SAT-solver resistance (§6.6). The differential analysis is stated to cover only the 64-bit output (§4.3: "our analysis of differential attacks in Section 6.2 only applies to the 64-bit case"). All claims are conditioned on a secret, random 256-bit key ("Our attack model assumes that the secret key is initially unknown", §6.1; README: "These security claims assume the seed is secret"). The README's "expected 2^32 guesses" collision figure is just the 64-bit birthday bound; no collision-probability bound below 2^-64 per pair is claimed or derived.

row.acknowledged_attacks: No cryptanalytic break of HighwayHash is acknowledged anywhere in the project's README, headers, paper or issue tracker (122 issues/PRs scanned, issues_all.tsv). Relevant discussions: Issue #28 "False security claims" (rurban, opened 2016-11-25, closed 2016-12-03) — disputes the hash-flooding/DoS framing ("Please refrain from using the false SipHash security claims and adding your own nonsense.") by arguing brute-force partial collisions on the low table-index bits and seed recovery; this concerns hash-table usage, not a break of the PRF; the maintainers replied "FYI we have studied differential/length extension/rotational/SAT solver attacks against HighwayHash without finding a weakness (paper pending publication)" (jan-wassenberg, 2016-11-25) and subsequently rewrote the README into the present "Defending against hash flooding" section (which now says a strong hash "is not, by itself, sufficient"). Issue #41 "It seems weak/zilch" (erthink, 2017-02-10, closed 2017-02-11) contains no attack ("Now i not ready to clear define/describe the proof, but it seems to poor, near to пшик/zilch"). Issue #17 "Publish the test suite/security metrics" (2016-08-03, still open) is where the arXiv preprint was announced (2016-12-27). The paper itself acknowledges limits: the differential analysis covers only the 64-bit output, and "HighwayHash needs further strengthening and analysis before it can serve as a cryptographically secure message digest" (§4.3). I did not survey the external cryptanalysis literature beyond the project's own sources.
row.notes: (1) Claim summary: HighwayHash is presented as a keyed "strong pseudorandom function" (highwayhash.h L87; paper abstract) whose "main claim" is indistinguishability from a uniformly random source, validated statistically rather than proven (paper §6). The only numeric collision statement is the README's 64-bit birthday figure ("an expected 2^32 guesses of `m`"), stated jointly for SipHash and HighwayHash and explicitly conditional on a secret seed; the paper additionally says 64-bit outputs "are not ‘collision-resistant’" and gives sqrt(pi/2 * 2^64) as the generic bound. For 128/256-bit outputs the paper disclaims: they "pass our test suite" but the differential analysis "only applies to the 64-bit case" and the function "needs further strengthening and analysis before it can serve as a cryptographically secure message digest" (§4.3, p.6). (2) Key/seed: the API takes a 256-bit key and no seed; SMHasher3 derives the key from a 64-bit seed (key lane i = (i+1) XOR seed), so its seed tests probe a 64-bit slice of the key space; mul0/mul1 are initialized from the fixed pi constants in both upstream and the port. (3) SMHasher3 marks the port FLAG_HASH_CRYPTOGRAPHIC and FLAG_IMPL_SLOW; the 238-test count is the slow-hash subset, not a failure count. The bulk figure (~2.9 bytes/cycle, sse41) corresponds to ~0.34 cycles/byte versus the README's 0.24 c/b AVX2 and 0.30 c/b SSE4.1 figures (README speed table, Xeon E5-2690 v3). (4) WebFetch refused to return the README verbatim, so upstream files were downloaded with curl and quoted from the saved copies; paper quotes come from pdftotext of v3 and page numbers were located by form-feed counting; one typeset radical is transcribed as sqrt(pi/2 * 2^64) and flagged as such in the location field. (5) Issue #28 was closed by the maintainers with a promise to moderate/split the discussion; jyrkialakuijala's comment listed "Clean up security claims in the documentation" as a follow-up topic, and the current README's hash-flooding section is the result. No issue reports a differential, collision or key-recovery attack on HighwayHash.
