claims.quote: SipHash-c-d with c ≥ 2 and d ≥ 4 is expected to provide the maximum PRF security possible (and therefore also the maximum MAC security possible) for any function with the same key size and output size. Our fast proposal is thus SipHash-2-4. We define SipHash-c-d for larger c and d to provide a higher security margin: our conservative proposal is SipHash-4-8, which is about half the speed of SipHash-2-4. We define SipHash-c-d for smaller c and d to provide targets for cryptanalysis. Cryptanalysts are thus invited to break • SipHash-1-0, SipHash-2-0, SipHash-3-0, SipHash-4-0, etc.; • SipHash-1-1, SipHash-2-1, SipHash-3-1, SipHash-4-1, etc.; • SipHash-1-2, SipHash-2-2, SipHash-3-2, SipHash-4-2, etc.; and so on.
claims.location: Paper §3 "Expected strength", p. 5 (siphash_paper.txt lines 244-256). Note: SipHash-1-3 has c = 1 < 2 and is therefore outside this claim; the paper never names "SipHash-1-3"

claims.quote: Note that the standard PRF and MAC security goals allow the attacker access to the output of SipHash on messages chosen adaptively by the attacker. However, they do not allow access to any "leaked" information such as bits of the key or the internal state. They also do not allow "related keys", "known keys", "chosen keys", etc.
claims.location: Paper §3 "Expected strength", pp. 5-6 (txt lines 257-263)

claims.quote: Of course, security is limited by the key size (128 bits). In particular, attackers searching 2^s keys have chance 2^(s−128) of finding the SipHash key. This search is accelerated in standard ways by speedups in evaluation and partial evaluation of SipHash, for one key or for a batch of keys; by attacks against multiple targets; and by quantum computers. Security is also limited by the output size (64 bits). In particular, when SipHash is used as a MAC, an attacker who blindly tries 2^s tags will succeed with probability 2^(s−64).
claims.location: Paper §3 "Expected strength", p. 6 (txt lines 264-271); superscripts written here with ^ because pdftotext flattens them ("2s keys have chance 2s−128")

claims.quote: We comment that SipHash is not meant to be, and (obviously) is not, collision-resistant.
claims.location: Paper §3 "Expected strength", p. 6, last sentence (txt lines 272-273)

claims.quote: High security. Our concrete proposal SipHash-2-4 was designed and evaluated to be a cryptographically strong PRF (pseudorandom function), i.e., indistinguishable from a uniform random function. This implies its strength as a MAC.
claims.location: Paper §1 Introduction, feature bullet list, p. 3 (txt lines 114-117)

claims.quote: Target applications include network traffic authentication and hash-table lookups protected against hash-flooding denial-of-service attacks. SipHash is simpler than MACs based on universal hashing, and faster on short inputs. Compared to dedicated designs for hash-table lookup, SipHash has well-defined security goals and competitive performance.
claims.location: Paper abstract, p. 1 (txt lines 14-20)

claims.quote: Key-recovery. Brute force will recover a key after on average 2^127 evaluations of SipHash, given two input/output pairs (one being insufficient to uniquely identify the key).
claims.location: Paper §5 "Preliminary cryptanalysis", p. 7 (txt lines 347-349); superscript flattened by pdftotext

claims.quote: Internal collisions. As for any MAC with 256-bit internal state, internal collisions can be exploited to forge valid tags with complexity of the order of 2^128 queries to SipHash. The padding of the message length forces attackers to search for collisions at the same position modulo 256 bytes.
claims.location: Paper §5 "Preliminary cryptanalysis", p. 8 (txt lines 359-362); superscript flattened by pdftotext

claims.quote: The best results were obtained by setting a 1-bit difference in the most significant bit of v3. After three iterations of SipRound many biases are found. But after four or more iterations we did not detect any bias after experimenting with sets of 2^30 samples.
claims.location: Paper §5, "Truncated differentials", p. 8 (txt lines 368-371)

claims.quote: Better characteristics may exist. However we expect that finding (collections of) characteristics that both have a high probability and are useful to attack SipHash is extremely difficult.
claims.location: Paper §5, "XOR-linearized characteristics", p. 8 (txt lines 393-395); preceded by the best characteristic found: probability 2^-134 for an omniscient attacker, 2^-159 over four rounds otherwise (txt lines 386-392)

claims.quote:
we proposed SipHash-2-4 as a (strong) PRF/MAC, and so far no attack whatsoever has been found,
although many competent people tried to break it. However, fewer rounds may be sufficient and I would 
be very surprised if SipHash-1-3 introduced weaknesses for hash tables.
claims.location: rust-lang/rust issue #29754 body (opened 2015-11-10 by funny-falcon), quoting an answer attributed to Jean-Philippe Aumasson; Aumasson (veorq) confirms below (comment 156073946, 2015-11-12): "SipHash designer here, haven't changed my opinion about SipHash-1-3 :-)"

claims.quote: A warning, though: SipHash-1-3 leaves 4 rounds between the last attacker-controlled input and the output. There's a "distinguisher" on 4 rounds in https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/722.pdf, or in simplest terms a statistical bias that shows up given a specific difference pattern in the input of the 4-round sequence. But you can't inject that pattern in SipHash-1-3 because you don't control all the state. And even if you could inject that pattern the bias wouldn't be exploitable anyway.
claims.location: rust-lang/rust issue #29754, comment by veorq (Aumasson), 2015-11-12

claims.quote:
This implementation is specifically for SipHash2-4 for a secure PRF

claims.quote: As I understand it, the 64-bit production version of SipHash is claimed to be as resistant as any other 64-bit MAC/PRF to attacks.  Is the security claim for the 128-bit version that it is as resistant as any other 128-bit PRF?

row.proof_offered: No proof. The paper's security section is titled "Expected strength" and phrases the claim as an expectation; the README repeats it verbatim ("is expected to provide the maximum PRF security"). Evidence offered is heuristic (§5 "Preliminary cryptanalysis"): generic bounds (key recovery 2^127 evaluations, state recovery ~2^191 SipRounds, internal collisions ~2^128 queries), truncated-differential experiments (biases after 3 SipRounds, none detected after 4 with 2^30 samples), the best XOR-linearized characteristic found (probability 2^-134 for an omniscient attacker who sees v3 every two rounds, 2^-159 over four rounds otherwise), verification that no vanishing xor-linear characteristic exists for 2-4 SipRounds, and a discussion of the zero-to-zero fixed point. The paper itself says "Better characteristics may exist." For SipHash-1-3 there is no security claim at all: c = 1 falls outside "c ≥ 2 and d ≥ 4", and the paper lists SipHash-1-x only as cryptanalysis targets; the sole designer statement is Aumasson's informal "I would be very surprised if SipHash-1-3 introduced weaknesses for hash tables" (Rust issue #29754, 2015). The README's only support beyond the claim is "no sign of weakness despite multiple cryptanalysis projects" with a link to eprint 2019/865.

row.acknowledged_attacks: The veorq/SipHash issue tracker (22 issues total, all listed in veorq_issues_all.txt) contains no reported attack, distinguisher, or weakness; the only security-related issue is #3 (2016-02-28, "Document the claimed security of the experimental 128-bit version"), resolved by extending the README claim (commit c03e6bb). The README acknowledges third-party cryptanalysis only in aggregate ("no sign of weakness despite multiple cryptanalysis projects"), with both links pointing to https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/865 — Le He and Hongbo Yu, "Cryptanalysis of Reduced-Round SipHash" (ePrint, "Preprint. MINOR revision."), whose abstract reports "distinguishers with practical complexity 2^{10} for SipHash-2-1 and 2^{36} for SipHash-2-2" and "a key recovery method for SipHash-2-1 that can obtain a nonuniform distribution of the 128-bit key through several bias tests"; nothing there reaches 2-4 or 1-3. Aumasson himself (Rust issue #29754, 2015-11-12) cites Dobraunig, Mendel, Schläffer, "Differential Cryptanalysis of SipHash" (SAC 2014, https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/722), abstract: "Our results are a characteristic for SipHash-2-4 with a probability of 2^{-236.3} and a distinguisher for the Finalization of SipHash-2-4 with practical complexity. Even though our results do not pose any threat to the security of SipHash-2-4, they significantly improve the results of the designers and give new insights in the security of SipHash-2-4."; he argues the 4-round finalization distinguisher is not injectable in SipHash-1-3. Not acknowledged by the project: Xin, Liu, Sun, Li, "Improved Cryptanalysis on SipHash" (CANS 2019, doi 10.1007/978-3-030-31578-8_4), which per its abstract (seen only via search summary, not verified verbatim) finds colliding and rotational-XOR-colliding characteristics for SipHash-1-x and SipHash-2-x instances. No practical attack on SipHash-2-4 or SipHash-1-3 is known or acknowledged; the kernel's characterization of SipHash1-3 as "an insecure PRF only suitable for hashtables" (Donenfeld 2017, reviewed by Aumasson) is a margin statement, not an attack.
row.notes: (1) Claim scope: the project's only formal claim is a PRF/MAC claim for c ≥ 2, d ≥ 4 with a secret 128-bit key, framed as an expectation ("Expected strength"); it explicitly disclaims collision resistance and keyless use. There is no claim of any kind for SipHash-1-3 in the paper or README; the variant name does not appear in either. (2) SMHasher3 tests only 64 of the 128 key bits (k1 = 0); a public-seed collision attack in SMHasher3's model therefore targets a keyspace the design never claims anything about, and the paper's model excludes leaked/known keys. (3) The README's "cryptanalysis projects" link points twice at the same eprint (2019/865), which attacks only SipHash-2-1 and SipHash-2-2. (4) The paper's quoted superscripts (2^127, 2^128, 2^30, 2^s) are flattened by pdftotext in siphash_paper.txt ("2127", "2s"); the PDF shows superscripts. (5) SMHasher3's reference implementation is Andrew Moon's floodyberry/siphash (frozen), tagged CRYPTOGRAPHIC; SipHash-2-4 is VERY_SLOW so its 3 Hashmap tests are skipped (235 vs 238). Speeds in the results table are for the [ssse3] build. (6) HalfSipHash (238/238, 81.75 cycles, 0.34 B/cycle) and TinySipHash (14 failures) are separate SMHasher3 entries and not part of this dossier. (7) The rurban "SipHash13" 0.9% figure is a BIC max-bias number that is smaller than the unflagged SipHash 2-4 value in the same test, so it should not be read as a quality defect specific to 1-3. (8) The CANS 2019 abstract was obtained via a search summary only; quote it from the Springer page before publishing.

row.seed_bits_api: Two 64-bit secrets: polymur_init_params(PolymurHashParams* p, uint64_t k_seed, uint64_t s_seed) -- header comment line 47: "Expands a 64-bit or 128-bit seed to a set of parameters for hash evaluation." -- or a single 64-bit seed via polymur_init_params_from_seed(p, uint64_t seed), which derives k_seed and s_seed as polymur_mix(seed + ARBITRARY3) and polymur_mix(seed + ARBITRARY4). The polynomial key k is rejection-sampled from k_seed to be a generator of the multiplicative group mod 2^61-1 with k^7 < 2^60 - 2^56; README states the resulting key space is "totient(2^61 - 2) * (2^60 - 2^56) / (2^61 - 1) ~= 2^57.4"; s is a full 64-bit secret (s = s_seed ^ ARBITRARY1). README line 65-66: "The proof of almost universality applies to both, but for the proof of almost pairwise independence to hold you must provide 128 bits of entropy." A separate 64-bit per-call `tweak` argument exists with no collision claims.

claims.quote: PolymurHash is a 64-bit [universal hash function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_hashing) designed for use in hash tables. It has a couple desirable properties:
claims.location: README.md, opening paragraph, lines 3-5 (line wraps joined with spaces)

claims.quote: It is **mathematically proven** to have a statistically low collision rate. When initialized with an independently chosen random seed, for any distinct pair of inputs `m` and `m'` of up to `n` bytes the probability that `h(m) = h(m')` is at most `n * 2^-60.2`. This is known as an almost-universal hash function. In fact PolymurHash has a stronger property: it is almost pairwise independent. For any two distinct inputs `m` and `m'` the probability they hash to the pair of specific 64-bit hash values `(x, y)` is at most `n * 2^-124.2`.
claims.location: README.md, '# PolymurHash' section, first bullet, lines 7-14 (line wraps joined with spaces)

claims.quote: Needless to say, PolymurHash passes the full [SMHasher suite](https://github.com/rurban/smhasher/) without any failures[*](https://github.com/rurban/smhasher/issues/114#issuecomment-1587631635). For the proof of the collision rate, see [`extras/universality-proof.md`](extras/universality-proof.md).
claims.location: README.md, end of '# PolymurHash' section, lines 46-49 (line wraps joined with spaces)

claims.quote: The proof of almost universality applies to both, but for the proof of almost pairwise independence to hold you must provide 128 bits of entropy.
claims.location: README.md, '## How to use it', lines 65-66
polymur-hash.h lines 51-53 (identical text in README.md '## How to use it' lines 70-72)

claims.quote: PolymurHash has strong collision guarantees for input chosen independently from its random seed. An interactive attacker however can craft its input based on earlier seen hashes. PolymurHash is **not** a cryptographically secure collision-resistant hash if the attacker can see (or worse, request) hash values at will. This is not a failure of the underlying hash, for example the well-known Poly1305 hash used to secure TLS suffers from the same problem. It solves this by hiding its hash values from attackers by adding an encrypted nonce acting as a one-time-pad.
claims.location: README.md, '## Resistance against cryptanalysis', lines 137-144 (line wraps joined with spaces)

claims.quote: PolymurHash is not intended to be used in a context where an attacker can see the hash values. Its main intended use case is as a hash function for DoS-resistant hash tables. However, a clever attacker might still acquire *some* information about the hash values by using side-channels such as hash table iteration order, or timing attacks on collisions.
claims.location: README.md, '## Resistance against cryptanalysis', lines 146-150 (line wraps joined with spaces)

claims.quote: The above process is by no means a strong multi-round cipher and would likely not hold up to proper cryptanalysis in a standard context. But the underlying structure is sound (e.g. the ChaCha cipher has the form `mix(secret + input) + secret` where `mix` is an unkeyed permutation), and I believe that extrapolating what little information you can get from side-channels to recover `k, s` to execute a HashDoS attack is difficult.
claims.location: README.md, '## Resistance against cryptanalysis', lines 161-166 (line wraps joined with spaces)

claims.quote: In other words, PolymurHash does not suffer from weak keys. As a trade-off our key space is slightly more limited: in combination with the fact we want `k^7 < 2^60 - 2^56` for efficiency reasons we get a total key space of `totient(2^61 - 2) * (2^60 - 2^56) / (2^61 - 1) ~= 2^57.4`.
claims.location: README.md, '## No weak keys', lines 194-197 (line wraps joined with spaces)

claims.quote: The proof below assumes that our secret key `k` was chosen uniformly at random from all possible `K`, which in [the readme](../README.md#no-weak-keys) is described to be roughly 2^57.4 possible keys. Furthermore, it assumes this random choice is independent from our input.
claims.location: extras/universality-proof.md, '# Proof of almost universality', lines 3-6 (line wraps joined with spaces)

claims.quote:
But `m` and `m'` were chosen independently from our secret key `k`. So the probability that the polynomial `f_m(k) - f_m'(k)` happens to have `k` as its root mod `p` is at most `(14 + n/7) / |K|` where `K` is the set of all possible keys. Ignoring the negligible constant 14, and given that we have roughly `2^57.4` possible keys, this gives us an overall collision bound of

    Pr[PH(m) = PH(m')] <= n/7 * 2^-57.4
    Pr[PH(m) = PH(m')] <= n * 2^-60.2
claims.location: extras/universality-proof.md, '### Collision bound', lines 112-119 (prose line wraps joined with spaces)

claims.quote:
But `k, s` were picked uniformly at random from a total key space of `2^57.4 * 2^64` values, thus giving us our bound

    Pr[H(m) = x  &&  H(m') = y] <= n/7 * 2^-121.4
    Pr[H(m) = x  &&  H(m') = y] <= n * 2^-124.2
claims.location: extras/universality-proof.md, '## Proof of almost pairwise independence', lines 158-163 (prose line wraps joined with spaces)

row.proof_offered: Yes, a written (non-machine-checked) proof: extras/universality-proof.md. Structure: (1) the input is injectively encoded as 56-bit words m[i] and then as a polynomial f_m(k) (block-Horner over 49-byte blocks, k^14 shift, three length-specific injective tail polynomials of degree < 14; length recovered from the k^1 coefficient and the block count from the top exponent); (2) for m != m' the difference f_m - f_m' is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most 14 + n/7 over GF(2^61-1), so it has at most that many roots; k uniform over ~2^57.4 admissible keys and independent of the input gives Pr[collision] <= (14 + n/7)/|K| ~ n * 2^-60.2; (3) adding the independent 64-bit s after the bijective mixer gives Pr[H(m)=x and H(m')=y] <= n * 2^-124.2 (almost pairwise / almost strongly universal). The final Murmur-style mix and +s are bijections, so they add no collisions. Caveats stated by the author: no formal verification, only a Python overflow/reduction simulation (bounds-check.py); in issue #7 (2023-09-02, open) he is "fairly confident" but knows of no external review; the pairwise-independence bound needs 128 bits of seed entropy (the 64-bit polymur_init_params_from_seed path, which is what SMHasher3 uses, only supports the almost-universal bound formally). For the interactive/cryptanalytic setting there is NO proof, only an informal argument: the README says the mix+s structure "would likely not hold up to proper cryptanalysis in a standard context" and offers only the belief that recovering k, s from side channels to mount HashDoS "is difficult".

What the project itself acknowledges: (a) README 'Resistance against cryptanalysis': not a cryptographically secure collision-resistant hash if the attacker can see or request hash values; an interactive attacker can craft inputs from seen hashes; side channels (iteration order, collision timing) may leak some information; the mix+s construction "would likely not hold up to proper cryptanalysis in a standard context". (c) Issue #7 (2023-09-02, still open): author confirms no known external review of the proofs. (d) Issue #8 (2023-12-24): avaneev disputes the "universal" wording; author clarifies the claim is almost-universality with the bound growing linearly in input length and that "There is no collision bound for a fixed key at all". row.notes: (1) Threat model of the proven bound: random secret (k, s) chosen independently of the inputs, attacker never sees outputs; the bound n*2^-60.2 is per pair of inputs of length <= n bytes and grows linearly with length (e.g. 2^-52.2 at 256 B, 2^-40.2 at 1 MiB, per orlp in issue #8). Effective polynomial key space is ~2^57.4 (not 2^61) because k is forced to be a group generator with k^7 < 2^60-2^56. (2) In the SMHasher3 'polymurhash' configuration the 64-bit seed is expanded to (k, s) by polymur_init_params_from_seed, so only the almost-universal bound applies formally (README: the pairwise-independence proof needs 128 bits of entropy). (3) polymurhash-tweakseed's SeedBIC failures are consistent with the project's explicit statement that no claims are made across different tweaks (the tweak is only added before the final mixer). (4) SMHasher3 tests v2.0-era code (upstream commit a7cc6b0); rurban's copy is a submodule pinned at tag v1.0 (commit ffe06d32); the only v1->v2 difference is the empty-string output (v1 returned a seed-independent value; v2 folds len=0 into the polynomial path), so speed/quality figures are comparable. (5) SMHasher3 speed numbers are from the upstream maintainer's x86 machine reported at 3.5 GHz in the raw file; the upstream README's own speed claim is "On an Apple M1 machine it can hash any input <= 49 bytes in 21 cycles, and processes 33.3 GiB/sec (11.6 bytes / cycle) for long inputs." (README lines 16-18). (6) Quotes taken from line-wrapped Markdown have their line breaks joined with single spaces and are otherwise verbatim (backticks, bold markers and link syntax preserved); the header-comment quote keeps its original line breaks. (7) The issue tracker is quiet since 2023-12; upstream repo has had no commits since 2023-06-23. (8) FLAG_HASH_XL_SEED in SMHasher3 denotes a hash whose seed is expanded by a separate seedfn into a larger parameter block (Hashinfo.h HASH_FLAGS list); SMHasher3 tests the 64-bit seed_t through that expansion.

row.seed_bits_api: Key = `struct umash_params` { uint64_t poly[2][2]; uint64_t oh[UMASH_OH_PARAM_COUNT + UMASH_OH_TWISTING_COUNT]; } with UMASH_OH_PARAM_COUNT = 32, UMASH_OH_TWISTING_COUNT = 2, i.e. 38 x 64-bit words = 304 bytes (2432 bits) of parameters: two polynomial multipliers f in Z/(2^61-1)Z stored as {f^2, f} (~61 random bits each) and 34 x 64-bit OH words (the README says "expanding each seed to a 320-byte key" for the demerphq SMHasher port). Filled either from random bytes via `umash_params_prepare` (failure probability "< 2**-110" for uniform input, umash.h line 209) or deterministically by `umash_params_derive(params, uint64_t bits, const void *key)` from a 64-bit value plus an optional 32-byte secret expanded with Salsa20 (NULL key -> the literal default secret "Do not use UMASH VS adversaries."). Separately, `umash_full`/`umash_fprint` take a per-call `uint64_t seed` that the authors say "is not associated with any collision bound" / "comes with no guarantee".
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64-bit seed_t in all four variants. UMASH-64 / UMASH-128 (no seedfn): one global `umash_params` derived once by umash_params_derive(bits=0, key=NULL) (umash_init, umash.cpp lines 1164-1167); SMHasher3's 64-bit seed is passed straight through as the `seed` argument of umash_full/umash_fprint (lines 1170-1189), i.e. the seed only exercises the argument the authors describe as having no collision guarantee. UMASH-64.reseed / UMASH-128.reseed ($.seedfn = umash_slow_reseed, lines 1157-1160): every seed change re-derives the full 304-byte parameter struct with umash_params_derive(seed, NULL) (Salsa20 expansion, default public secret) into a thread-local table and also passes the same 64-bit value as base_seed for the `seed` argument. Both paths are deterministic functions of the 64-bit SMHasher3 seed.
row.output_bits: 64 (umash_full, `which` = 0 or 1 selects one of the two hashes); 128 (umash_fprint = struct umash_fp { uint64_t hash[2]; }, two 64-bit hashes computed concurrently). README also states both 32-bit halves pass rurban/demerphq SMHasher. SMHasher3 tests $.bits = 64 (UMASH-64, UMASH-64.reseed) and $.bits = 128 (UMASH-128, UMASH-128.reseed).

claims.quote: UMASH provably avoids parameter-independent collisions.  For any two inputs of `s` bytes or fewer, the probability that a randomly parameterised UMASH assigns them the same 64 bit hash value is less than `ceil(s / 4096) 2**-55`.

claims.quote: # UMASH: a non-cryptographic hash function with collision bounds

claims.quote: UMASH is a fast (9-22 ns latency for inputs of 1-64 bytes and 22 GB/s peak throughput, on a 2.5 GHz Intel 8175M) 64-bit hash function with mathematically proven collision bounds: it is [ceil(s / 4096) * 2^{-55}]-almost-universal for inputs of s or fewer bytes.

claims.quote: When that's not enough, UMASH can also generate a pair of 64-bit hashes in a single traversal.  The resulting fingerprint reduces the collision probability to less than [ceil(s / 2^{26})^2 * 2^{-83}]; the probability that two distinct inputs receive the same fingerprint is less 2^{-83} for inputs up to 64 MB, and less than 2^{-70} as long as the inputs are shorter than 5 GB each.  This expectation is taken over the randomly generated `umash_params`.  If an attacker can infer the contents of these parameters, the bounds do not apply.

The seed and secret are expanded into random bytes with Salsa20; the resulting `umash_params` should be practically random, as long the seed or secret are unknown.

claims.quote: The universal collision bounds for UMASH hold under the assumption that keys are fully re-generated with random bytes, independently of the hash function's inputs. While UMASH accepts a 64-bit "seed" value, it is merely a hint that we would like to see different hash values, without any guarantee. Nevertheless, this suffices to pass SMHasher's seed-based collision tests. For real guarantees, expand short keys into full UMASH keys with a stream cipher like Salsa20.
claims.location: umash.pdf ('UMASH: a fast almost universal 64-bit string hash', Paul Khuong, Backtrace I/O, 2022-02-23), page 1, abstract, second paragraph

claims.quote: UMASH should not be used for cryptographic purposes, especially not against adversaries that can exploit side-channels or adapt to the hashed outputs, but it does provide worst-case pair-wise collision bounds. For any two strings of s bytes or fewer, the probability of them hashing to the same value satisfies ε < ⌈s/4096⌉ · 2^−55, as long as the independently generated key is chosen uniformly at random. However, once a few collisions have been identified (e.g., through a timing side-channel in a hash table), the linearity of the hash function makes it trivial to combine them into exponentially more colliding values.

claims.quote: UMASH may also generate a 128-bit fingerprint by computing a secondary hash value concurrently with the usual (primary) UMASH value; the combination of the two 64-bit values guarantees a collision probability less than 2^−83 for input size up to 64 MB, and less than 2^−70 at 5 GB.

claims.quote: Our MIT-licensed UMASH hash function is a decently fast non-cryptographic hash function that guarantees a worst-case bound on the probability of collision between any two inputs generated independently of the UMASH parameters.

claims.quote: What sets UMASH apart from these other non-cryptographic hash functions is its proof of a collision probability bound.  In the absence of an adversary that adaptively constructs pathological inputs as it infers more information about the randomly chosen parameters, we know that two distinct inputs of \(s\) or fewer bytes will have the same 64-bit hash with probability at most \(\lceil s / 2048 \rceil \cdot 2^{-56},\) where the expectation is taken over the random "key" parameters.

For example, the linear structure of UMASH (and of other polynomial hashes like CLHash) makes it easy to combine known collisions to create exponentially more colliding inputs.  There is no universal answer; UMASH is simply another point in the solution space.

claims.quote: These collision bounds hold for all inputs constructed without any feedback about the randomly chosen UMASH parameters.

row.proof_offered: Yes, a written universal-hashing argument (the README calls it "a proof sketch for the collision bound"; umash.h calls the bounds "mathematically proven"). umash.pdf (rendered from umash_reference.py, 2022-02-23, 24 pages) gives: (i) short inputs (<= 8 bytes): SplitMix64-style invertible mixer with a per-length random parameter, "universal, never collides values of the same size, and otherwise collides values with probability ε_short ≈ 2^-64" (p. 2); (ii) block compressor OH = PH (carry-less NH/CLNH) for all but the last 16-byte chunk plus ENH for the last, shown 2^-63-almost-universal by a three-case analysis (pp. 5-6); (iii) Carter-Wegman polynomial hash over Z/(2^61-1)Z with degree d = 2*ceil(s/256), giving ε_poly ≈ d/(2^61-1), "conservatively" rounded to the claimed ε < ceil(s/4096)*2^-55 (p. 6); (iv) fingerprint: a second, twisted OH compressor and independent polynomial, with the case analysis 'The two easy cases' / 'The last, harder case (subcase a/b)' (pp. 9-12) giving ε_fp < ceil(s/2^26)^2 * 2^-83. The model is explicit: expectation over uniformly random, input-independent keys; the per-call 64-bit seed carries no bound; no security claim is made against adaptive adversaries or side channels (paper abstract, umash.h lines 26-27). The argument is prose/hand analysis, not machine-checked; the author's 2020-10-31 post admits an earlier fingerprint claim rested on an asserted property that "was slightly off" and reverted to "an older proof with weaker bounds".

row.acknowledged_attacks: No issue in the tracker reports a break of the stated bound (14 issues total, all closed; list saved in issues_list.txt). What the project itself acknowledges: (1) Paper abstract, p. 1: "However, once a few collisions have been identified (e.g., through a timing side-channel in a hash table), the linearity of the hash function makes it trivial to combine them into exponentially more colliding values." and "UMASH should not be used for cryptographic purposes, especially not against adversaries that can exploit side-channels or adapt to the hashed outputs". (2) umash.h lines 26-27: "If an attacker can infer the contents of these parameters, the bounds do not apply." (3) Blog 2020-08-24: "the linear structure of UMASH (and of other polynomial hashes like CLHash) makes it easy to combine known collisions to create exponentially more colliding inputs." (4) Default secret literal "Do not use UMASH VS adversaries." (umash.h line 224; umash.c line 1047; also used by SMHasher3). (5) Self-corrected proof gap: pvk.ca post 2020-10-31 'Nearly double the PH bits with one more CLMUL': "Turns out the part where I simply asserted a property was slightly off 😉. I had to go back to an older proof with weaker bounds, but that's not catastrophic: we still collide way more rarely than \(2^{-70}\)." The 2020-08-24 announcement stated fingerprint bound ceil(s/2048)^2 * 2^-112 and 64-bit bound ceil(s/2048)*2^-56; the current README/paper state ceil(s/2^26)^2 * 2^-83 and ceil(s/4096)*2^-55. (6) Issue #18 (tczajka, 2022-02-13, https://github.com/backtrace-labs/umash/issues/18, 'Incorrect comparison to hardware failure probability'): objected to the doc sentence "anything stronger than $\approx 2^{-70}$ is dominated by hardware failure, incinerated datacenters, or war." with "if you fingerprint about 2^{35} items with that collision probability, you will start getting collisions."; pkhuong replied 2022-02-13: "You're right that the birthday bound works like that, and I was being aggressive in that statement. I will definitely rephrase in the upcoming documentation re-edit." (closed 2022-02-18). (7) Issue #35 (michaeleisel, 2023-09-04, https://github.com/backtrace-labs/umash/issues/35): asks whether two independently parameterised UMASH hashes give ceil(s/4096)*2^-110; pkhuong (2023-09-05): "The answer is yes, the collision probabilities for independently generated parameters do multiply independently… but maybe you want a cryptographic hash? And also, you have to square the size of the input too." (8) Issue #15 (pkhuong, 2020-10-29, design note): using xor instead of addition inside ENH was rejected because "`(m ^ k) - k` is xor-linear in `k` [...], i.e., very predictable." and "at that point, an attacker simply has to make sure `c' = c - d`."
row.notes: (1) UMASH IS in SMHasher3 (hashes/umash.cpp, four registered variants), contrary to the hint; it sits in the 'Failing hashes' tables, not the passing table. (2) The failure pattern tracks the authors' own caveat: the non-reseed variants feed SMHasher3's 64-bit seed only into the per-call `seed` argument that the docs say "comes with no guarantee", and 91 of their 127/128 failures are Seed* tests (SeedSparse, SeedBlockLen, SeedBlockOffset, Seed, SeedAvalanche, SeedBIC, SeedBitflip) plus PerlinNoise; the .reseed variants, which regenerate the full key from the seed via Salsa20, drop to 36/37 failures, all in fixed-key tests (BIC at 3/4/6/8 bytes, Zeroes, Sparse, Permutation, Bitflip-4, SeedZeroes) that are identical in both modes because seed 0 gives the same key. These are statistical distribution/BIC/collision-count failures (e.g. Zeroes: 15 actual 64-bit collisions vs 0.0 expected; Sparse 2/2048: 13280 vs 0.0), not demonstrations that the almost-universal bound is violated; SMHasher3's expectations are for an idealised random function, whereas UMASH promises only ceil(s/4096)*2^-55 per pair. (3) The bound's threat model is explicit and narrow: keys uniformly random and independent of the inputs; no claim against adaptive adversaries, side channels, or key inference; the paper says linearity lets known collisions be combined into exponentially many more. (4) The default 32-byte secret in umash_params_derive is the public string "Do not use UMASH VS adversaries.", which is what SMHasher3 uses; a key derived from a public secret plus a 64-bit `bits` value has at most 2^64 possibilities, a setting the authors' own blog distinguishes from their model (their pigeonhole remark on 64-bit-seed hashes). (5) Numbers drifted across versions: 2020-08-24 blog ceil(s/2048)*2^-56 and fingerprint ceil(s/2048)^2*2^-112 (better than 2^-70 to 7.5 GB); current README/umash.h/paper ceil(s/4096)*2^-55 and ceil(s/2^26)^2*2^-83 (< 2^-70 up to 5 GB/GiB; README says 'GiB', umash.h and paper say 'GB'). The paper's change log records PH->OH (2020-10-13) and a tightened fingerprint analysis (2022-02-14); the 2020-10-31 post records a retracted assertion. (6) Minor SMHasher3 README vs raw discrepancies: UMASH-64 avg cycles 41.73 (README) vs 41.74 (raw 'Average'); UMASH-128.reseed bulk 3.79 (README) vs 3.80 (raw 'Average'), 3.79 ('Alignment rnd'). (7) Paper quotes: the PDF typesets ⌈s/4096⌉ and 2^−55; pdftotext renders them as 'ds/4096e · 2−55' (see umash_paper.txt lines 24, 271, 562); the quotes above restore the symbols, everything else is verbatim. README quotes keep the raw-markdown double spaces after periods. (8) Upstream also cites Yves Orton's demerphq SMHasher (extended seeds to a 320-byte key) as passing; not independently verified here. (9) Rust port mentioned in README: https://github.com/backtrace-labs/umash-rs (not examined).

row.hash: ChainHash (paper hash of "Fast Evaluation of Polynomials with Rational Preprocessing"; SMHasher3 registrations chainhash-256 and chainhash-1k) together with the underlying injective three-key recurrence rows ("This paper, one chain / 8 lanes, F_2^64"; "This paper, F_2^89-1")
row.version: No version number. Two definitions exist, same proofs/bounds/key size: (a) arXiv:2609.06022v1 (submitted 5 Sep 2026) documents the adjacent word pairing with the byte length XORed into the last a_i only (SMHasher3 verification LE 0xDE1AB9F9 chainhash-256 / 0x32B4EE71 chainhash-1k; Table 2 rows 61.7/40.5, 57.7/36.8, 26.6/27.4 GB/s); (b) the current definition, local repo commit 370c3d1 (2026-09-06, "strided word pairing with the length in both halves of the last pair (new definition)") and the public fork commit c7947d25 on gitlab.com/lobais/smhasher3 branch mr/chainhash (author date 2026-09-05 09:47, committer date 2026-09-06 00:23; git describe release-25-gc7947d25 on top of upstream 3b619371 of 2026-08-27): verification LE 0xAA4E2A3B / BE 0x11037F6F (chainhash-256), LE 0x7A1ED2E0 / BE 0x85B2F299 (chainhash-1k). Shipped configurations ChainHash<32,5,1> = chainhash-256 (256-byte blocks, S=1) and ChainHash<128,5,2> = chainhash-1k (1 KB blocks, two 512-byte sub-blocks); a 64-byte-block row (W=8, 17 key words) is timed in the paper but not registered in SMHasher3.

row.seed_bits_api: Ideal key of the theorems: W+9 independent uniform GF(2^64) elements = 41 words (2624 bits) for 256-byte blocks, 137 words (8768 bits) for 1 KB blocks, 17 words (1088 bits) for 64-byte blocks (block key k_0..k_{W-1}, recurrence keys u,y,z, finalizer c_0..c_4, twist t_in). The shipped implementation (chainhash.h setup(), and the SMHasher3 seedfn) derives all of them from ONE 64-bit seed with splitmix64 -- a 2^64-member subfamily the paper says its theorems do not cover (Remark 15 (A1)). Injective recurrence rows: 3 key words (u,y,z) for "one chain" (64 bits proven), 4 words for "8 lanes" (61 bits), 5 words for the F_{2^89-1} variant (88 bits), 1 word for the single-key specialization y=x^3,z=x,u=x^2.
row.seed_bits_smhasher3: 64: `static uintptr_t chainhash_seed_init(const seed_t seed)` casts the seed_t to uint64_t and runs splitmix64 BLOCK_WORDS+9 times (k[], u, y, z, c[0..4], t_in) into a thread_local key; the hash function "ignores the seed value, because it uses a separate seeding function; the seed argument is the pointer returned by it" (hashes/chainhash.cpp L943-963). Registered $.bits = 64, hash_flags FLAG_HASH_CLMUL_BASED, impl_flags FLAG_IMPL_MULTIPLY_64_64 | FLAG_IMPL_LICENSE_BSD (portable backend adds FLAG_IMPL_VERY_SLOW).
row.output_bits: 64 (one GF(2^64) element; $.bits = 64 in both registrations). The injective-recurrence F_{2^89-1} row outputs the full 89-bit residue; the paper records that truncating it to 64 bits is unsafe.

claims.quote: Theorem 11 (Collision bound). Fix W, S and n ≥ 1, and put p = Sn. For every two distinct messages m ≠ m′ with n(m), n(m′) ≤ n (equivalently: of at most nB bytes each), Pr_{κ,θ,c,τ}[H_{κ,θ,c,τ}(m) = H_{κ,θ,c,τ}(m′)] ≤ (p+2)/2^64 = (Sn+2)/2^64.
claims.location: arXiv:2609.06022v1, Appendix J.2 'Statement', Theorem 11, p. 171 (pdftotext line 8730); LaTeX source sections/appendix_chainhash.tex L231-238 (thm:ph:collision); math rendered in plain text, wording verbatim

claims.quote: For the 256-byte configuration this reads (⌈ℓ/256⌉ + 2)/2^64 for messages of at most ℓ bytes, and for the 1 KB configuration (2⌈ℓ/1024⌉ + 2)/2^64: 3/2^64 and 4/2^64 for messages of up to 256 bytes, 4098/2^64 ≈ 2^−52 and 2050/2^64 ≈ 2^−53 for messages of up to 1 MB.
claims.location: arXiv v1 Appendix J.2, sentence after Theorem 11, p. 171 (pdftotext lines 8738-8741); appendix_chainhash.tex L240-244

claims.quote: Theorem 12 (5-wise independence up to level-1/2 collisions). Fix W, S, n ≥ 1, p = Sn, and t ≤ 5 pairwise distinct messages m_1, . . . , m_t with n(m_i) ≤ n. Let D be the event (determined by (κ, θ)) that the level-2 values V_κ(m_1), . . . , V_κ(m_t) are pairwise distinct, i.e. that no pair suffers an E_1 or E_2 collision. Then (i) Pr[¬D] ≤ C(t,2) (p+1)/2^64; (ii) conditioned on any (κ, θ) ∈ D and on any τ, the vector (H(m_1), . . . , H(m_t)) is uniform on F^t: the outputs are independent and uniform, in particular 5-wise independent; (iii) consequently, for every T ⊆ F^t, |Pr[(H(m_1), . . . , H(m_t)) ∈ T] − |T|/2^64t| ≤ C(t,2) (p+1)/2^64.
claims.location: arXiv v1 Appendix J.7, Theorem 12 (pdftotext lines 9138-9150); appendix_chainhash.tex L703-717 (thm:ph:kwise); binomial written C(t,2)

claims.quote: The collision probability is at most (p + 2)/2^64 for two messages of at most n blocks, p = Sn sub-blocks: 2^−64 for the block level (the full-width XOR-universality of carryless NH, extended to last blocks of different pair counts by the length term), p/2^64 for the recurrence (the three-key bound above, with p counting sub-blocks rather than word pairs) and 2^−64 for the finalizer (Section J). No heuristic mixing step is used anywhere, and both variants pass all 200 tests of the full SMHasher3 suite, on an Apple M2 Pro and on an Intel Xeon 8375C, including a new seeded-differential test (full-output collisions of structured pairs, complemented leading or adjacent interior words, over 2^24 random seeds, 2^30 in an extended tier) that MUM fails outright and wyhash, rapidhash, XXH3 and XXH3-128 fail in the extended tier, while komihash, Polymur, SipHash and the polynomial hashes pass (Section I).
claims.location: arXiv v1 Section 3, paragraph 'A large-key hash built from the recurrence', p. 19 (pdftotext lines 866-876); sections/injective.tex L396-409

claims.quote: The ChainHash bounds (Section J) are proved for a key of W + 9 independent uniform field elements; the implementation timed and tested here expands a 64-bit seed with splitmix64, a 2^64-member subfamily that the theorems do not cover (Remark 15).
claims.location: arXiv v1 Table 2 caption, p. 18 (pdftotext lines 820-822); sections/injective.tex L313-317 (caption of tab:injective:adversarial)

claims.quote: (A1) Ideal key. Theorems 11 and 12 are about the family indexed by a uniform (κ, θ, c, τ) ∈ F^{W+9} (8(W + 9) random bytes; 328, 1,096 and 136 bytes for W = 32, 128, 8). The implementation derives (κ, θ, c, τ) from a 64-bit seed with splitmix64; the resulting 2^64-member subfamily is not covered by the theorems (no pseudorandomness assumption is made or needed for the ideal-key statements; cf. the counting argument of [LK16, §2.5]).
claims.location: arXiv v1 Appendix J.9, Remark 15 'Assumptions, and the gap between the theorem and the code', item (A1) (pdftotext lines 9451-9457); appendix_chainhash.tex L1098-1105 (rem:ph:gaps)

claims.quote: (A2) Exact field arithmetic. gfmul is assumed to be the field product in F_2[X]/(Π) (irreducibility of Π: [LK16, §4.3], re-checked in tools/bench/chainhash/sanity.py); the fast and reference multiplies are compared in test T7, and the fast hash against the bit-serial reference in tests T1/T4 of test_chainhash.cpp. Equivalence of chainhash.h with Definition 11 is tested, not proved.
claims.location: arXiv v1 Appendix J.9, Remark 15 item (A2) (pdftotext lines 9459-9463); appendix_chainhash.tex L1106-1111

claims.quote: Any fixed bijection of the finalizer input preserves the 2^−64 bound and the 5-wise independence exactly, and the carry chain of an integer addition is not F_2-affine (Section J.8); with the twist the degree-5 hash passes 200/200, degree 3 with the twist still fails 17, and whether the twist suffices for a given test suite is an empirical question, not a theorem.
claims.location: arXiv v1 Section 3, p. 19 (pdftotext lines 861-865); sections/injective.tex L383-390

claims.quote: We adopt the standard model for keyed hashing: the secret key material is drawn uniformly at random and hidden from the attacker, who chooses the input messages. The quantity of interest is the worst case, over attacker-chosen inputs, of the collision probability taken over the random secret. A universal hash bounds this by a small ε for every input pair; a heuristic hash need not.
claims.location: arXiv v1 Section 3, paragraph 'Comparison with general-purpose hashes', p. 15 (pdftotext lines 724-728); sections/injective.tex L259-264

claims.quote: In the three-key family P_n is monic of degree n in y with the message-independent top part (z + u)y^n (see the end of the proof of Lemma 1), so the difference of two such polynomials has total degree at most n, and the family is n/|F|-almost universal on messages of 2n field elements: half of Horner's bound at half of Horner's multiplications, with three resident key words. In the single-key specialization P_n has degree 3n + 2 and its three leading coefficients are again the same for every message, so the difference has degree at most 3n − 1 and the family is (3n − 1)/|F|-almost universal with one key word.
claims.location: arXiv v1 Section 3 'Injective Polynomial Hashing with Fewer Multiplications', after Definition 2, p. 12 (pdftotext lines 552-561); sections/injective.tex L39-40

claims.quote: With the three-key recurrence in every lane the bounds tighten to (⌈N/L⌉ + L − 1)/|F| for a shared key triple plus one combining key and ⌈N/L⌉/|F| for independent triples per lane (messages of equal length).
claims.location: arXiv v1 Section 5.10, paragraph 'Injective-Lanes' (pdftotext lines 1627-1629); sections/experiments.tex L630-633 -- the bound behind the 'This paper, 8 lanes' row (key 4 words, 61 bits)

claims.quote: Replacing the field multiplication by the "MUM" fold lo_64(ab) ⊕ hi_64(ab) of the 128-bit product makes the bulk throughput 9× higher (14.4 bytes/cycle), but that variant is not a field operation: the fold is many-to-one, so the injectivity argument of this section and the Schwartz–Zippel collision bound do not apply to it, and message sets with elevated collision rates exist. We report the number only to locate the cost of exact field arithmetic; the guarantees of this section are for the field version.
claims.location: arXiv v1 Section 3.1 'Experiments', p. 14 (pdftotext lines 697-703); local sections/injective.tex L189-197 gives 14.1 bytes/cycle instead of 14.4

claims.quote: What the experiments establish is a lower bound of order 2^−27 (wyhash, rapidhash, XXH3) and 1 (MUM) on the worst case, against a proven upper bound of n/2^64 for the three-key field version of our hash on n word pairs ((3n − 1)/2^64 with a single key word).
claims.location: arXiv v1 Appendix I, paragraph 'Caveat', p. 168 (pdftotext lines 8565-8568); sections/appendix_adversarial.tex L184-197

claims.quote: Add ChainHash, a provably universal 5-independent 64-bit hash
claims.location: Commit title, branch mr/chainhash of the author's public SMHasher3 fork (2026-09-05/06); body: "Collision probability for two messages of at most p pairs is <= (p + 2) / 2^64.  The twist is a bijection of the finalizer input, so it changes neither the bound nor the 5-wise independence." and "There is no heuristic mixing step anywhere."

claims.quote: Results (Apple M2 Pro, Apple clang 17, PMULL backend, full suite): both variants pass 200/200.  Bulk speed (256 KB keys): 22.2 and 17.3 bytes/cycle; small keys (1-31 B): 72 and 77 cycles/hash. Results (Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C, clang 21, PCLMULQDQ backend): both pass 200/200, identical verification codes; bulk 15.4 and 12.3 bytes/cycle; small keys 108 and 109 cycles/hash.
claims.location: Commit message, final paragraph (fork_commit_c7947d25_message.txt in the claims directory)

claims.quote: The cycle counts are those of the block level and tail loader of the time of the experiment; the optimised implementation shipped since (Remark 15(A7)) computes the same function bit for bit and measures 66 cycles per small key (72 for the 1 KB configuration) and 20.7 (17.5) bytes/cycle in bulk in the same benchmark (SMHasher3's own, on 256 KB keys; the harness figures of Table 2 use 16 KB messages and order the two configurations the other way).
claims.location: arXiv v1 Appendix J.8 'Measurements' (pdftotext lines 9250-9255) -- numbers of the adjacent-pairing definition; the local (unpublished) appendix_chainhash.tex L847-849 reads '72 cycles per small key (77 for the 1 KB configuration) and 22.2 (17.3) bytes/cycle'

row.proof_offered: Yes, full proofs. Appendix J (arXiv v1 pp. 170-180; local sections/appendix_chainhash.tex) proves the three levels separately: Lemma 58 (CLNH is 2^-64-XOR-universal on 128 bits, full width), Lemma 59 (distinct messages give distinct streams w.h.p., handles unequal lengths/pair counts via the length XOR), Lemma 60/61 (injectivity of the recurrence restated with an explicit pivot decoder, three-variable Schwartz-Zippel, level-2 collision ≤ (p+1)/2^64), Lemma 62 (the degree-5 three-multiplication characteristic-2 circuit is a bijective parametrisation of monic quintics, with an explicit unit-pivot decoder), Lemma 63 (finalizer collision 2^-64 on distinct inputs), Lemma 64/Corollary (any fixed bijection of the finalizer input, in particular the integer-add twist, is free); Theorem 11 (collision ≤ (Sn+2)/2^64) and Theorem 12 (5-wise independence conditioned on level-1/2 distinctness). Injective recurrence: Lemma 1 (injectivity via explicit coefficient extraction) plus Schwartz-Zippel gives n/|F| (three keys), (n+1)/|F| (two keys), (3n-1)/|F| (single key); lane forms bounded in Section 5.10. Verification scripts named: verify5.py, exh5.c, sanity.py, test_chainhash.cpp T1-T9. Explicit scope limits (Remark 15): proofs are for the ideal W+9-word key, not the splitmix64-expanded 64-bit seed; equivalence of code and definition is tested, not proved; the twist's adequacy for SMHasher3 is "an empirical question, not a theorem". No DoS-resistance claim is made beyond the keyed-adversary model; no pseudorandomness assumption is made.

The table does not list any hash function named ChainHash, chainhash, injective-hash, or 'Ahle.'" (saved copy rurban_README.md in the claims directory).
row.acknowledged_attacks: No published attack on ChainHash exists or is acknowledged; there is no issue tracker for the hash (the fork commit is the only public artifact; no upstream MR). The project itself records: (1) SMHasher3 failures of rejected variants -- untwisted degree-5 finalizer fails 22/200 (Zeroes, Sparse, Permutation, TwoBytes, Bitflip; worst bias 195.9x on a 16-bit window of Permutation), twisted degree-3 fails 17/200, the interim strided variant with the length XORed into a only failed the Zeroes keyset (199/200) -- all fixed by the shipped design and explained as F_2-degree structure (Appendix J.8, Remark 'The length XOR'); (2) the seeded interface is a 2^64-member subfamily "not covered by the theorems" (Remark 15 A1), and the twist's adequacy for any test suite is "an empirical question, not a theorem"; (3) the 'MUM-fold' variant of the plain recurrence port (injective-hash.mum) is explicitly excluded from the Schwartz-Zippel guarantee and fails the extended seeded-differential tier at 15/2^30 (MANIFEST section 10) -- that is not the field version; (4) the open 'Key expansion' problem: deriving the O(B) NH key from a k-wise polynomial gives key-free collisions for reduced NH ("for k = 6 we verified that such a pair of 38-word blocks has the same difference under 200 random seeds"), and for the unreduced carryless NH used here "We found no better attack, but also no proof; the security of unreduced NH under k-wise independent keys is an open problem (Section 6)"; (5) truncating the F_{2^89-1} recurrence output to 64 bits collides at 2^-25 for a pair differing by 2^64-1 in the last word, so the Mersenne rows output the full residue.
row.notes: 1) Public vs. local versions differ: arXiv:2609.06022v1 (5 Sep 2026; PDF date line says '9th September 2026') documents the adjacent-pairing definition (length in a_i only; Table 2: 61.7/40.5, 57.7/36.8, 26.6/27.4 GB/s at 16 KB/512 B; SMHasher3 66/72 cycles, 20.7/17.5 B/cycle). The local tree (commit 370c3d1, 2026-09-06, not yet on arXiv) and the public fork commit c7947d25 carry the strided definition with the length in both halves (Table: 69.3/39.2, 67.7/37.6, 27.5/29.4 GB/s; SMHasher3 72/77 cycles, 22.2/17.3 B/cycle). Proofs, key size (W+9), the (p+2)/2^64 bound and 5-wise independence are unchanged; only the CLNH constant in the stream lemma changes to (l+l')(1+X^64). Blog quotes should be taken from v1 or flagged as 'repository, unpublished'. 2) The 'bits' column: ChainHash 62 = 64 - log2(3) from the shortest-message bound 3/2^64; the injective rows are 64 (one chain, n/|F|), 61 (8 lanes, key 4 words, Section 5.10 lane bound) and 88 (F_{2^89-1}, 89-bit output). 3) SMHasher3 numbers are the author's own fork runs; nothing is in upstream fwojcik results or rurban's README, and no upstream MR exists (GitLab API checked 2026-09-17; the only lobais MR is !29 poly_mersenne). The fork branch and commit are publicly viewable. 4) The paper's claim 'ChainHash show[s] no collision in 2^30 seeds' (Appendix I) rests on extended-tier runs of 2026-09-03 whose logs are labelled degree-3 (sd_chainhash-256.txt) and degree-7 (-k7-s1) builds, i.e. earlier finalizers, not the shipped degree-5+twist strided definition; the shipped definition was seeded-differential-tested only at the default 2^24 tier inside the 200-test full-suite runs (final6 logs line 2439-2448, 0 collisions) and in the 2026-09-04 default-tier sweep (degree-7 build). 5) The plain-recurrence SMHasher3 port numbers disagree between v1 (1.59 B/cycle, 133 cycles, 14.4 for the MUM fold) and the local injective.tex (1.49, 142, 14.1); MANIFEST section 8 marks those logs 'Untraceable'. 6) DoS resistance is never claimed in those words; the security statement is the keyed-adversary collision bound above, valid only for the ideal key -- with the 64-bit splitmix64 seed the family is 2^64 members and the paper explicitly declines to claim anything for it. 7) Cost: n*S recurrence multiplications + 3 finalizer multiplications + 2*ceil(len/32) carryless products per message; the shipped M2 implementation pins PMULL/PMULL2 via inline asm. 8) The claims scratchpad directory already contained files from another agent (cnt_*.txt, *.sections, rurban_README.md, smhasher3_logs/); mine are the ones listed under files.
